aarons-rod-and-the-bronze-serpent-nehush.context_blurb: Aaron was Moses's older brother and the first high priest of Israel. The book of Numbers tells two strange wonder-stories that gather around a wooden staff. In the first, during the wilderness years after the Exodus, the tribes of Israel grumble again against the priesthood and God sends a sign through the night in the sacred Tent of Testimony to settle who should serve as priest. In the second, after further rebellion, a plague of biting serpents breaks out in the camp and Moses is told to mount a bronze healing-sign on a pole where every bitten person can look at it. Centuries later a reforming king of Judah has to deal with the sign all over again when his people begin treating it as an idol. The two stories are told in Numbers 17 and 21, with the sequel in 2 Kings 18.

abraham-called-from-ur-to-canaan-and-the.context_blurb: The book of Genesis opens the family-saga of Israel with an old man named Abram, his wife Sarai, and his nephew Lot. God calls them out of a great walled city in the ancient Near East and tells them to walk hundreds of miles into a land they have never seen. From that call unfolds the long chain of promises, name-changes, and strange encounters that make up the founding chapters of the Hebrew Bible — three visitors who sit under a tree at the oaks of Mamre, a mysterious priest-king at Salem, and the destruction of the cities of the plain. The whole span is told in Genesis 11 through 19 KJV.

the-binding-of-isaac-on-mount-moriah.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God tests the old patriarch Abraham by commanding him to take his son — the long-awaited child of promise he had waited decades for — up a mountain in the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt sacrifice. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, cuts the wood for the fire, and walks three days with the boy and two young servants. The moment the angel calls down from heaven at the last second echoes through the New Testament and the Quran. Source: Genesis 22 KJV.

jacobs-ladder-at-bethel-and-the-wrestlin.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, Isaac's younger son is a schemer. He first cheats his elder twin out of the firstborn's blessing by bringing their old blind father a cooked meal under a disguise. Fleeing his brother's rage, he lies down in the desert with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a stairway reaching from earth to heaven with angels moving up and down it. Years later, coming home with wives and children, he spends a whole night by a small river wrestling a mysterious stranger. He walks away with a limp, a new name, and the identity his descendants will carry forever. Sources: Genesis 25–32 KJV.

josephs-coat-of-many-colors-and-the-pit-.context_blurb: Jacob loved his son Joseph more than any of his other children because Joseph was the son of his old age, born late in life to his beloved wife Rachel. To mark him as the favored son Jacob gave him a striking garment the elder brothers hated him for. Joseph then made it worse by telling his family the dreams he kept having — dreams of sheaves and stars bowing down to him. The ten older brothers finally caught him alone in a pasture at Dothan and threw him into a dry pit while they argued what to do with him. Source: Genesis 37 KJV.

joseph-reveals-himself-i-am-joseph-your-.context_blurb: Years after being sold into slavery, Joseph has risen to the highest post in Egypt beneath Pharaoh. Famine has reached Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons south to buy grain. They bow before the Egyptian vizier they do not recognize — the brother they threw into a pit more than twenty years before. Joseph puts them through a series of hard tests before the moment of recognition that is one of the great reunion scenes in the Hebrew Bible. Source: Genesis 42–45 KJV.

moses-in-the-basket-of-bulrushes.context_blurb: A new Pharaoh has arisen in Egypt who did not know Joseph. He enslaves the Hebrews and orders a horror against every newborn Hebrew boy. A Levite woman gives birth to a healthy son and hides him for as long as she can — then floats him down the Nile in a waterproofed basket of reeds, with the baby's older sister watching from the bank. The scene opens the whole Exodus story. Source: Exodus 1–2 KJV.

the-burning-bush-and-the-name-i-am.context_blurb: Years after fleeing Egypt as a young man, Moses has become a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law. He leads the sheep to the backside of the desert and comes to the mountain of God, where he sees a bush that is on fire but is not being burned up. The voice that speaks from the bush gives him both his life's work and the great mysterious name of God that the Hebrew Bible treats as holiest of all. Source: Exodus 3–4 KJV.

the-ten-plagues-of-egypt.context_blurb: The book of Exodus tells how Moses and his brother Aaron go before Pharaoh and demand that the Hebrews be let out of Egypt. Each refusal brings a plague — ten in all, each worse than the last — that batter the land, the water, the livestock, and finally the firstborn of Egypt. Pharaoh breaks and lets them go, and the Hebrews march out carrying unleavened bread and bitter herbs for a Passover meal that would be kept once a year ever after. Source: Exodus 5–12 KJV.

the-parting-of-the-red-sea.context_blurb: The Hebrews have marched out of Egypt and are camped at the edge of the Red Sea when Pharaoh changes his mind one last time and sends his chariots after them. Moses stretches out his hand with his staff; God sends a wind that blows all night; the waters stand up on both sides and the Hebrews walk through on dry ground. When the Egyptian chariots follow in after them, the walls of water come back down. Source: Exodus 14 KJV.

sinai-the-tablets-and-the-golden-calf.context_blurb: Three months out of Egypt, the Hebrews reach the foot of a mountain in the Sinai wilderness. Thunder, cloud, and the long blast of a trumpet come down on it. Moses climbs up alone and stays forty days and forty nights. He comes down carrying two stone tablets inscribed by the finger of God — and finds that in his absence, Aaron and the people have made themselves a different god of molten gold. Source: Exodus 19–32 KJV.

noah-and-the-ark-the-raven-the-dove-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God sees that the whole human race has grown wicked and resolves to wipe it from the earth with a great flood. He chooses one man — Noah — and tells him to build a wooden ark, and to bring his family and pairs of every kind of animal onto it. Rain falls, the fountains of the deep break open, the ark floats, and when the waters finally begin to go down Noah sends out two different birds in turn to see whether dry land has come back. Source: Genesis 6–9 KJV.

hagar-and-ishmael-sent-into-the-wilderne.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, Sarah has waited years for a child of her own and still has none. She hands her Egyptian handmaid Hagar to Abraham as a second wife so that he may have a son. Hagar bears him his first son, and years later — after Sarah has her own son by a miracle — the family fractures. Sarah demands that Hagar and the boy be sent away; Abraham sends them off with a loaf and a bottle of water. Alone in the wilderness of Beersheba, the water runs out. Source: Genesis 16, 21 KJV.

deborah-barak-sisera-and-jaels-tent-peg.context_blurb: In the book of Judges, Israel is being terrorized by the Canaanite general Sisera, who commands a fleet of nine hundred iron chariots. A prophetess who judges Israel from under a certain tree in the hills of Ephraim summons the war-captain Barak and gives him God's order to march north. Barak will go — but only on a strange condition. The battle that follows ends twice — once at the river Kishon, and once hours later in the tent of a woman named Jael. Source: Judges 4–5 KJV.

gideon-the-fleece-the-three-hundred-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Judges, the Midianites' camel-raids have driven Israel into caves. An angel finds Gideon of Ophrah hiding to beat out his wheat in an unexpected place and greets him as 'thou mighty man of valour.' Gideon asks for sign after sign to be sure the call is real, then whittles his army down from thirty-two thousand men to a famous small number for the night raid on the Midianite camp. Source: Judges 6–7 KJV.

samson-the-honey-in-the-lion-the-jawbone.context_blurb: In the book of Judges, an angel visits the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah and tells her the son she will bear must be a Nazarite from the womb — sworn to God his whole life, forbidden ever to let a razor touch his head. He grows up to be the strongest and strangest of Israel's judges, a one-man wrecking crew against the Philistines who makes riddles, tears a lion apart with his bare hands, and finally brings down a pagan temple on his own head. Source: Judges 13–16 KJV.

ruth-gleaning-in-the-field-of-boaz.context_blurb: The book of Ruth opens in the days of the Judges, when a famine drives a Bethlehemite named Elimelech to leave Israel with his wife Naomi and their two sons. The family settles in a neighboring country east of the Dead Sea, where the sons both marry local women. When all three men die, Naomi walks home empty-handed; one of her foreign daughters-in-law refuses to be sent away and walks beside her. The rest of the book is about how that foreign widow is gathered into Israel in a barley-field at Bethlehem. Source: Ruth KJV.

joshua-at-jericho-the-trumpets-and-the-w.context_blurb: After Moses dies on Mount Nebo in sight of the Promised Land but never entering it, one man takes his place and leads Israel across the Jordan on dry ground. Their first target is Jericho, a walled city sitting on the plain. Before the attack two spies slip inside, find shelter in a surprising house, and promise its mistress a sign of safety for her family when the city falls. Source: Joshua 2–6 KJV.

the-defeat-at-ai-and-joshuas-long-day.context_blurb: Fresh from the fall of Jericho, Joshua expects an easy second win against the small nearby city of Ai. The Israelite force is routed, and the question is why. The problem turns out to be a man named Achan, who had taken plunder from Jericho that was supposed to belong to God alone. Later in the same campaign, Joshua is caught in a long day of fighting against five southern kings and prays for the sun and moon to stand still until the battle is finished. Source: Joshua 7, 10 KJV.

choose-you-this-day-whom-ye-shall-serve-.context_blurb: In the Hebrew Bible book of Joshua, the warrior-leader who took Moses's place at the Jordan has grown old. He gathers all the tribes of Israel to the ancient covenant-town of Shechem for a farewell speech. The most quoted line from that speech — 'but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' — has gone around the world. After his death the Israelites also bury a set of very old bones they had carried out of Egypt forty years before. Source: Joshua 24 KJV.

david-and-goliath.context_blurb: In 1 Samuel 17 of the Hebrew Bible, the Philistine army and the Israelite army are camped on two facing hills with a broad valley between them. Every morning for forty days a Philistine giant named Goliath strides down into the valley and shouts for any Israelite brave enough to meet him in single combat. A young shepherd named David arrives on an errand carrying food for his older brothers in the Israelite camp, and steps forward with nothing in his hand but his sling and five smooth stones from the brook. Source: 1 Samuel 17 KJV.

david-and-jonathan-the-sworn-brotherhood.context_blurb: In the books of Samuel, Jonathan, the eldest son and crown prince of King Saul of Israel, loves the young David as his own soul from the day David strikes down Goliath. The two make a secret covenant of brotherhood, even though David is destined to take the throne Jonathan should have inherited. Saul grows jealous and tries to kill David, and Jonathan risks his own neck to warn his friend by a signal in a field. When Jonathan dies in battle on Mount Gilboa years later, David's funeral song over him and his father is one of the most moving laments in the Hebrew Bible. Source: 1 Samuel 18–20; 2 Samuel 1 KJV.

david-and-bathsheba-and-nathan-the-proph.context_blurb: In 2 Samuel 11 of the Hebrew Bible, King David of Israel is at ease in his palace while his army is off besieging the Ammonite capital of Rabbah on the far side of the Jordan. One evening David gets up from his bed and walks on the flat palace roof. Looking down over the wall he sees a beautiful woman in the courtyard below. The prophet Nathan's parable the next chapter, the loss of a baby, and David's famous seven-day fast all follow from what the king does next. Source: 2 Samuel 11–12 KJV.

elijahs-mantle-and-the-harp-of-david-the.context_blurb: In the Hebrew Bible, the young shepherd David is summoned to King Saul's court because the king is being tormented by a spirit that makes him rage. David plays a stringed instrument for him and the king is refreshed and the evil spirit departs. Later, in 1 Kings 19, the old prophet Elijah walks up to a young farmer named Elisha who is plowing his father's field and throws his hairy prophet's garment across the young man's shoulders. The garment becomes one of the great symbols of prophetic succession in the Hebrew Bible. Sources: 1 Samuel 16; 1 Kings 19 KJV.

elijah-at-cherith-and-zarephath-the-rave.context_blurb: The prophet Elijah the Tishbite stands before King Ahab of Israel and swears that there will be no dew and no rain in the land except by his word. God then tells him to slip away and hide by a brook east of the Jordan, and sends creatures to feed him there morning and evening. The drought that follows runs for several years, and the New Testament later cites its exact length twice. Along the way Elijah lodges with a starving widow in a foreign town, where a jar of meal and a cruse of oil never run empty. Sources: 1 Kings 17; Luke 4; James 5 KJV.

mount-carmel-elijah-and-the-prophets-of-.context_blurb: After three years of drought, the prophet Elijah challenges King Ahab's four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal to a showdown on the top of Mount Carmel. Each side builds an altar, lays a bull on it, and calls on its god to answer by fire. Elijah pours water three times over his altar until a trench around the stones is full before he even prays. Source: 1 Kings 18 KJV.

horeb-the-still-small-voice-the-fiery-ch.context_blurb: Hours after fire fell on his sacrifice at Carmel, the prophet Elijah learns that Queen Jezebel has sworn by her gods to have him killed by the next day. He runs for his life a day's journey into the wilderness and sits down under a lonely tree to die. Instead he is fed by an angel, walks forty days and forty nights to the mountain where Moses once met God, and hears the Lord in an unexpected form — not in wind, earthquake, or fire. The chapter closes with his final journey and the strange way he leaves this world. Source: 1 Kings 19; 2 Kings 2 KJV.

elisha-the-double-portion-the-bears-and-.context_blurb: The young farmer Elisha has just been called from his father's plow by the old prophet Elijah. To show he is not going back, he kills his own oxen and gives his village a farewell feast — burning the equipment of his old life as the cooking-fire. The rest of 2 Kings is a sequence of his famous miracles: a floating iron axe-head, a Syrian commander's cure, a dead boy raised by lying on him and sneezing seven times, and even one strange story that keeps working after Elisha himself is already dead and buried. Source: 2 Kings 2–13 KJV.

jonah-the-great-fish-nineveh-and-the-gou.context_blurb: The Hebrew Bible book of Jonah tells how God sent a reluctant prophet east to call the wicked Assyrian capital of Nineveh to repent. Jonah does not want to go. He goes down to the Mediterranean port of Joppa, pays his fare, and boards a ship sailing the opposite way, toward far Tarshish. The great storm, the lots, the swallow by a great fish, the second call, and the quarrel at the end over a gourd-vine are all in the book's four short chapters. Source: Jonah 1–4 KJV.

daniel-in-the-lions-den.context_blurb: In the reign of King Darius the Mede over Babylon, the elderly prophet Daniel keeps on quietly praying three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem. His enemies at court trick the king into signing an edict that anyone who prays to any god but the king for thirty days will be killed. When Daniel refuses to stop praying, Darius is forced to seal him overnight in a pit of hungry wild beasts. Source: Daniel 6 KJV.

belshazzars-feast-and-the-writing-on-the.context_blurb: In the Hebrew Bible book of Daniel chapter 5, a Babylonian king throws a drunken banquet for a thousand of his lords. His guests are drinking wine from gold cups his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had looted from the Temple in Jerusalem. In the middle of the party, something impossible appears in mid-air near the great lamp of the hall and begins to write words directly on the plaster of the wall. The old prophet Daniel is summoned to read what it says. Source: Daniel 5 KJV.

nebuchadnezzars-dream-and-the-fiery-furn.context_blurb: King Nebuchadnezzar, the mightiest ruler of the ancient world, has torn Daniel and his three Jewish friends out of Judah and marched them east into captivity. The king first dreams a great statue made of several different metals in layers, and only Daniel can tell him both the dream and its meaning. Later the king sets up a huge golden image on the plain of Dura, orders every subject to bow when the music plays, and when Daniel's three friends refuse he throws them into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. Source: Daniel 2–3 KJV.

esther-mordecai-haman-and-the-feast-of-p.context_blurb: The Hebrew Bible book of Esther is set in the Persian capital of Shushan under King Ahasuerus. Queen Vashti is deposed for refusing to be paraded before the drunken Persian lords, and a beauty search across the empire turns up a young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, raised by her cousin Mordecai. She is brought to the palace and crowned queen under a Persian name. Then a vizier named Haman proposes to kill every Jew in the empire — and Queen Esther has to risk her neck to speak for her people. Source: Esther 1–10 KJV.

isaiah-coals-to-the-lips-and-the-seraphi.context_blurb: In the sixth chapter of the Hebrew Bible book of Isaiah, a young prophet in Jerusalem stands in the Temple in the year King Uzziah dies and sees the Lord sitting upon a throne 'high and lifted up.' The hem of the robe alone fills the whole Temple. Six-winged burning ones hover above the throne crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' The prophet cries out that he is undone, a man of unclean lips — and one of the burning ones flies to him with a coal from the altar. Source: Isaiah 6 KJV.

jeremiah-the-potters-wheel-and-the-linen.context_blurb: In the days of King Josiah of Judah, the Lord calls a young priest's son of Jerusalem to be the prophet to a kingdom staggering toward destruction by Babylon. His call-scene, his tour of a working potter's shop, his object-lessons with a hidden linen belt and a smashed earthen jar, his imprisonment at the hands of his own countrymen, and the Ethiopian servant who hauls him up out of a mud-pit by old rags under the arms are all in the book that carries his name. Source: Jeremiah 1–38 KJV.

ezekiel-the-wheel-and-the-valley-of-dry-.context_blurb: By the river Chebar in Babylon, a young exile priest sees the heavens open in his thirtieth year — a cloud from the north with fire enfolding itself and brightness round about it. He becomes the strangest visionary in the Hebrew Bible. His wheels within wheels, his vision of a valley of dry bones that come back together bone to bone, his siege-models and his lying on his side for forty days are all gathered in the book that bears his name. Source: Ezekiel 1, 37 KJV.

samuel-anointing-saul-and-later-david.context_blurb: Before he was ever born, the prophet Samuel was promised to God by a barren mother who had wept and prayed at the shrine of Shiloh until the priest Eli mistook her silent moving lips for drunkenness. Samuel grew up to be the last of the judges of Israel and the kingmaker who anointed its first two kings — first a tall Benjaminite who hid among the baggage out of embarrassment, and then, long after the first king had been rejected, a young shepherd summoned in from the pasture by Samuel at Jesse's house in Bethlehem. Sources: 1 Samuel 1, 10, 16 KJV.

solomon-wisdom-the-two-mothers-the-templ.context_blurb: In 1 Kings of the Hebrew Bible, the young king Solomon — son of David by Bathsheba — goes up to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice. That night God appears to him in a dream with a startling offer: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Instead of long life or riches, Solomon asks for one thing, and his wisdom becomes famous across the ancient world. The two mothers before his throne, the building of the Temple in Jerusalem, and the visit of the Queen of Sheba all follow from that early choice. Source: 1 Kings 3–10 KJV.

solomons-temple-menorah-showbread-and-th.context_blurb: In 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, King Solomon builds in Jerusalem the first great Temple of God in Israel. For seven years and more he gathers cedar from Lebanon, hammered gold, olivewood for the giant inner cherubim, and twelve brazen oxen to carry the molten sea. The Holy Place has a seven-lamped golden lampstand, a table of showbread, and ten lavers for washing; and the inmost chamber shelters the Ark of the Covenant with the tablets from Mount Horeb. Sources: 1 Kings 6–8; 2 Chronicles 3–7 KJV.

bethlehem-the-manger-and-the-shepherds.context_blurb: In the Gospel of Luke's Christmas story, Mary and Joseph are on the road because the emperor in Rome has ordered a headcount of the whole empire and everyone has to travel to their family's home town to be counted. Joseph's family town is Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judea. When Mary's time comes to give birth, the newborn ends up laid in an animal's feed-trough — and Luke states the plain reason in the famous Nativity line. The scene then opens out onto a hillside outside the town, where shepherds hear singing in the sky. More than a thousand years later Francis of Assisi staged the first live Christmas scene around a similar hilltop village in Italy. Source: Luke 2 KJV.

gabriel-to-mary-and-the-leap-in-elizabet.context_blurb: In the first chapter of the Gospel of Luke, an angel appears to a young woman named Mary in a house in Nazareth in Galilee. He greets her with 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' and tells her she will bear a son called Jesus. Mary asks a single startled question in reply. The scene then crosses the hill country of Judea to the house of Mary's older kinswoman Elizabeth, whose own long-barren pregnancy with the future John the Baptist has already made the elderly priest Zacharias mute. Source: Luke 1 KJV.

the-magi-the-star-herod-and-the-flight-t.context_blurb: Matthew's Gospel opens its Nativity story with strangers walking into Jerusalem from a long way east. They go straight to the palace of King Herod the Great and ask the question that terrifies him — where is the newborn king of the Jews? They explain how they knew to come at all. Herod sends them on to Bethlehem with orders to come back and tell him what they find; instead they go home another way, and the holy family flees south to escape what Herod does next. Source: Matthew 2 KJV.

the-boy-jesus-in-the-temple-at-twelve.context_blurb: Only one of the four Gospels gives any scene from Jesus's childhood after the Nativity itself. Luke tells how his parents went every year to a great feast in Jerusalem, and the one year they lost him on the trip home. They turn back and look for a day and a half, and finally find him in the Temple — sitting among the teachers of the Law. The scene closes with the first words of Jesus the gospels record. Source: Luke 2:41–52 KJV.

john-the-baptist-locusts-honey-and-the-d.context_blurb: Out in the desert country east of Jerusalem, a wild preacher stands by the river and calls the crowds to turn their lives around. He dresses like the old Hebrew prophets — a rough coat and a leather belt — and eats whatever the wilderness provides. He is the long-promised son of the old priest Zacharias and his wife, named by an angel at Zacharias's altar of incense. One day his young kinsman Jesus walks down out of Galilee to be baptised by him in the river, and a voice from heaven speaks over the water. The baptizer later loses his head at Herod's birthday banquet in Machaerus. Source: Matthew 3, 14; Luke 1 KJV.

forty-days-in-the-wilderness-the-three-t.context_blurb: Right after his baptism in the Jordan, Jesus goes out alone into the wilderness. He eats nothing for a set stretch of time that Matthew and Luke both give the same figure for. The devil then meets him there, and tests him three times — one test with hunger, one with power, and one with a leap from a dizzying height. Each test ends with Jesus answering by quoting a line of Deuteronomy from memory. Source: Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13 KJV.

water-into-wine-at-the-wedding-in-cana.context_blurb: At a village wedding in Galilee, Jesus, his mother Mary, and his new disciples are all guests. Partway through the feast the wine runs out, which in that honor-conscious culture would be an acute humiliation for the host family. Mary goes to her son. The six large stone jars standing nearby at the door were meant for ceremonial washings; Jesus has them filled with water, and sends a sample to the master of the feast. The sign — the first of seven 'signs' in John — opens Jesus's public ministry. Source: John 2 KJV.

the-sermon-on-the-mount-and-the-beatitud.context_blurb: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus climbs a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, and before he begins his longest single teaching he takes the posture a rabbi always used when teaching students. The sermon that follows runs three chapters and contains some of the most famous lines of Western literature — the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the lily of the field, the Golden Rule, and the house built on sand. Source: Matthew 5–7 KJV.

the-sower-and-the-mustard-seed.context_blurb: Jesus pushes a small fishing boat a little way out from the shore of the Sea of Galilee, sits down in it while the crowd stands on the beach, and opens a parable with a farmer image. Later in the same chapter he gives another parable about the smallest of all garden seeds growing into a tree where the birds come and lodge. The 'kingdom of heaven' chain in Matthew 13 and Mark 4 is one of Jesus's great teaching sequences. Source: Matthew 13; Mark 4 KJV.

the-good-samaritan-on-the-jericho-road.context_blurb: A lawyer tries to test Jesus by asking who exactly counts as his 'neighbor.' Jesus answers with a story. He sets it on a specific road — a man traveling downhill from Jerusalem — a road that dropped more than three thousand feet in just over fifteen miles, perfect ambush country. Three different people pass the half-dead victim before the one who finally stops. Source: Luke 10:25–37 KJV.

the-prodigal-son-the-ring-the-sandals-an.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells a parable that opens with a plain one-line setup: 'A certain man had two sons.' The younger boy walks up to his father one morning with a demand that would have shocked every listener at the time. He goes off to a far country, spends what his father gave him, ends up feeding animals Jews considered unclean — and finally comes to himself, rehearsing a short speech on the long walk home. The father's answer and the complaint of the older brother who stayed are the heart of the parable. Source: Luke 15:11–32 KJV.

the-lost-sheep-and-the-lost-coin.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells three parables that are all about finding what was lost. The first is a shepherd who has a hundred sheep and finds that one has strayed. The second is a woman with ten silver coins who sweeps the whole house for the one that fell out of her head-dress. Each parable ends the same way — joy, calling in the neighbors, the simple triumphant line that heaven rejoices in the same way. Source: Luke 15:1–10 KJV.

lazarus-and-dives-and-the-sheep-and-the-.context_blurb: Jesus tells a parable in Luke 16 about two men who die on the same day. One is a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen who feasts every day at his own table; the other is a poor beggar covered in sores who lies outside the rich man's gate hoping for the scraps that fall. The parable turns everything upside down after death. In Matthew 25 Jesus gives another vision of the final judgment — a shepherd separating two kinds of animal — that has worked on Christian imagination ever since. Sources: Luke 16; Matthew 25 KJV.

the-talents-and-the-ten-virgins.context_blurb: In a pair of parables in Matthew 25, Jesus tells of a rich man who entrusts different sums of money to three of his servants before a long journey, and of ten young women waiting at night with lamps for a bridegroom's wedding procession. Both are parables about being ready. Source: Matthew 25:1–30 KJV.

come-forth-raising-jairuss-daughter-and-.context_blurb: The Gospel of Mark introduces a desperate father who falls at Jesus's feet at the start of one healing scene — a local synagogue-ruler whose only daughter is dying at home. The Gospel of John tells a longer, slower raising scene later in Jesus's ministry: his friend Lazarus of Bethany has already been in the tomb for days when Jesus finally arrives, and his sisters Martha and Mary each meet him on the road out. Sources: Mark 5; John 11 KJV.

five-loaves-and-two-fishes-feeding-the-f.context_blurb: Late one afternoon on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, a huge crowd has followed Jesus into a lonely, grassy place and has nothing to eat. The disciples want to send them home to buy supper; Jesus tells them to feed the crowd themselves. The miracle begins with the lunch of one small boy and ends with a specific count of baskets gathered afterwards. The scene is the only one of Jesus's miracles that all four gospels record. Sources: Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9; John 6 KJV.

the-storm-on-the-sea-and-walking-on-the-.context_blurb: The disciples Peter, Andrew, James, and John worked as commercial fishermen on the same lake Jesus later crossed many times with them. On one crossing Jesus slept through a violent storm in the stern of their boat; the terrified disciples woke him. On another night the disciples were in the boat alone when a figure walked out across the waves toward them, and Peter asked to walk out and meet him. Sources: Mark 4:35–41; Matthew 14:22–33 KJV.

the-paralytic-through-the-roof-and-blind.context_blurb: Jesus is teaching inside a packed house in Capernaum, and four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend on his sleeping mat. The crowd at the door is too tight to push through — so they find another way in. Later in Mark's gospel, Jesus is leaving the city of Jericho surrounded by a huge following when a blind beggar sitting by the road hears who is passing and shouts out his own name over and over, refusing to be hushed. Sources: Mark 2; Mark 10 KJV.

the-transfiguration-on-the-mountain.context_blurb: The gospels say Jesus led a small group of his closest disciples up a high mountain, apart from the rest. There his clothes began to shine, and two long-dead figures from the Hebrew Bible appeared with him on the mountainside. A cloud came and covered them, and a voice spoke out of the cloud. The three disciples came down the mountain in silence. Sources: Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9 KJV.

palm-sunday-and-the-whip-of-cords.context_blurb: On the Sunday before his death, Jesus sends two disciples ahead of him into a village just outside Jerusalem to find and bring back a particular animal tied up near a door. He rides down the Mount of Olives into the city on it as the crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road. Days later, in the Temple itself, he drives out the money-changers and the sellers of sacrificial animals with a scourge of small cords. Sources: Matthew 21; John 2 KJV.

the-last-supper-the-kiss-and-let-this-cu.context_blurb: In an upper room in Jerusalem on the night before Passover, Jesus eats the Passover meal with the Twelve. Partway through the meal he tells them that one of the men eating with him will betray him, and as they go around the table they each begin to ask the same short, worried question. Later that same night in a garden across the Kidron Valley, Jesus prays three times under the olive trees while his closest three disciples cannot stay awake, and the betrayer finally arrives at the head of an arresting party with a single pre-arranged signal. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18 KJV.

peters-denial-and-the-cock-crowing.context_blurb: On the night Jesus is arrested and taken to the high priest's house for questioning, one of his closest disciples follows the arresting party at a distance and slips into the courtyard. The servants and guards there have kindled a fire against the cold, and the disciple stands among them warming his hands. Three different people recognise him through the course of the night, and each time he insists he does not know Jesus — until a bird crows just before dawn. The last scene of John's gospel reconciles the same disciple to Jesus by a very similar charcoal fire. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18, 21 KJV.

pilate-the-crown-of-thorns-and-what-is-t.context_blurb: Dragged by the Jewish authorities at dawn to the Roman governor's residence in Jerusalem, Jesus is questioned by the Roman prefect of Judea. The governor's opening question cuts straight to the political charge: 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' Jesus does not deny it. The soldiers plait a crown out of thorn-branches, dress him in a scarlet robe, and the governor finally offers the crowd a choice between Jesus and a prisoner named Barabbas. Sources: Matthew 27; John 18–19 KJV.

simon-of-cyrene-the-seven-last-words-and.context_blurb: On the walk out of Jerusalem toward the execution ground, Jesus is too exhausted to carry the crossbeam alone. Roman soldiers grab a random bystander from the crowd and force him to shoulder it. Mark's gospel names him in one phrase. At the hill called Golgotha a sign in three languages is hung above the cross, and across the three hours of darkness the four gospels together record a handful of famous last sayings — including a Hebrew cry from Psalm 22 and a single Greek word meaning 'it is finished.' Sources: Mark 15; John 19 KJV.

joseph-of-arimathea-and-the-empty-tomb.context_blurb: The afternoon of the crucifixion, a wealthy member of the Jewish ruling council walks in to see the Roman governor Pilate and boldly asks for the body of Jesus. Mark's gospel calls him 'an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God.' He takes the body down, wraps it in a linen sheet, and lays it in his own new-cut rock tomb in a garden nearby. Early on the first morning after the Sabbath, three women walk to that tomb carrying spices — and find the great stone already rolled away. Sources: Mark 15–16; John 19–20 KJV.

emmaus-doubting-thomas-and-the-153-fish.context_blurb: After the resurrection, two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus about seven miles away. A stranger falls in beside them and walks and talks with them for nearly the whole seven miles — and they never realise who he is until he breaks bread at their table that evening. Days later, in another appearance, Jesus comes through locked doors to the Eleven and the once-doubting disciple Thomas sees him for himself. The last chapter of John takes the risen Jesus back to the shore of the Sea of Tiberias and a charcoal fire. Sources: Luke 24; John 20–21 KJV.

andrew-and-the-x-shaped-cross-of-patras.context_blurb: Andrew was a Galilean fisherman and the brother of Simon Peter. In the Gospel of John he appears as one of the very first men ever to follow Jesus — leaving John the Baptist on the banks of the Jordan to spend the day with the new rabbi. The Eastern Orthodox churches give him a one-word Greek title that no other apostle shares. Later Christian tradition sends him preaching through Greece and finally has him crucified in the city of Patras on a cross of a very particular shape. His relics, by medieval legend, were carried shipwrecked to a cold northern coast where his cross-shape still flies on the national flag. Sources: Gospel of John 1 and 6.

bartholomew-flayed-alive-in-armenia.context_blurb: Bartholomew is one of the twelve apostles Jesus of Nazareth chose, named in the gospel lists of Matthew, Mark, and Luke always paired with the apostle Philip. Later Christian tradition identifies him with the Nathanael of John's Gospel and sends him preaching to Greater Armenia, where he dies a particularly gruesome martyr's death. His flayed skin becomes one of the most arresting images in Western religious art — Michelangelo painted it in a famous and shocking way on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel. His feast falls in late summer. Sources: Synoptic gospel lists; Golden Legend.

matthew-the-tax-collector-at-the-receipt.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles had a job before he was called that made his neighbours despise him: he sat at a customs booth on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee, collecting taxes for Rome. Jesus walked past, said two words, and the man got up and left his table. The scene has been painted many times — most famously by Caravaggio, in a huge canvas for a chapel in the French church in Rome. By tradition the same man wrote the first of the four gospels in the New Testament. Sources: Matthew 9:9; Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27 KJV.

philip-and-nathanael-under-the-fig-tree.context_blurb: The day after John the Baptist first pointed Jesus out at the Jordan, Jesus met a young man from Bethsaida — the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew — and called him with two words: 'Follow me.' This young apostle immediately went to find his skeptical friend sitting under a tree and brought him to Jesus. Jesus greeted the friend as an Israelite in whom there was no guile, and said he had seen him under that tree before the two of them ever met. Source: John 1:43–51 KJV.

thomas-the-twin-put-your-finger-here-and.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles is introduced in the Gospel of John by a Greek nickname that means 'the twin.' He is the disciple who was not with the others on the first Easter evening when the risen Jesus appeared in the locked room, and who refuses to believe them. A week later Jesus comes back through the door with him there, and offers him the physical sign he had demanded. Later Christian tradition carries this apostle farther east than any of the others, as far as the Malabar Coast of India. Sources: John 20:24–29 KJV; Acts of Thomas.

simon-the-zealot-and-thaddaeus-the-two-l.context_blurb: Every Gospel list of the Twelve Apostles ends the same way: two names paired together just before Judas Iscariot. The second-to-last is a Simon — not Peter, a different one — carrying a one-word tag that would eventually become his standard name. The one just ahead of him is a figure called Thaddaeus (and in some lists Lebbaeus or Judas not Iscariot). Later tradition pairs them together on missionary journeys; one of them becomes the great Western patron of lost or impossible causes. Sources: Matthew 10; Mark 3; Luke 6 KJV.

james-son-of-zebedee-the-first-apostle-k.context_blurb: The apostle James, son of Zebedee, worked with his father and his brother John in a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee before Jesus called them. Jesus gave the two brothers together a joint Aramaic nickname — 'sons of thunder.' In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I begins persecuting the Jerusalem church and has this apostle killed by the sword. He becomes the very first of the Twelve to die for his faith. Later Spanish legend brings his body to the far northwest corner of Iberia, where a famous pilgrimage shrine still bears his name. Sources: Mark 1:19; Acts 12 KJV.

james-the-just-the-fullers-club-at-the-t.context_blurb: A man named James, called 'the Just' or 'the Righteous,' is identified in Mark 6:3 as a brother of Jesus of Nazareth. In the book of Acts he becomes the chief figure of the Jerusalem church — the one Peter and Paul report to, and the one who finally decides the Gentile question at the Jerusalem Council. By tradition he wore no wool, drank no wine, and had calloused knees from a lifetime of kneeling to pray. Josephus and the second-century historian Hegesippus both record his violent death. Sources: Acts 15; Josephus Antiquities 20.

judas-iscariot-the-thirty-pieces-the-kis.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve disciples went in the week of Passover to the chief priests and arranged to hand Jesus over to them, for a price that Matthew's gospel takes straight from the prophet Zechariah. In the garden of Gethsemane the betrayal is sealed with a pre-arranged signal — a single gesture at close range. Matthew and Acts give two different versions of what happens to the money and to the betrayer afterwards; both end in a field known locally by an Aramaic name meaning 'the field of blood.' Sources: Matthew 26–27; Acts 1; Zechariah 11 KJV.

peters-chains-the-angel-in-the-cell-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I has just put the apostle James the son of Zebedee to death with a sword, and seeing that this pleased the people he also arrests Peter and locks him up in prison chained between two soldiers, with four squads of soldiers assigned to guard him in turn. During the night an angel appears in the cell, taps Peter awake, and leads him out. Meanwhile the Jerusalem church is praying for him at the house of Mary the mother of John Mark — and a young servant-girl named Rhoda is the first to hear his knock at the gate. Source: Acts 12 KJV.

pentecost-the-wind-the-fire-and-the-thre.context_blurb: Fifty days after Passover, in the opening chapters of the book of Acts, about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus are shut in a single upper room in Jerusalem. A sudden sound as of a rushing mighty wind fills the house, and a flame as of a small tongue of fire comes to rest over the head of each of them. They go out into the street and begin to speak, and every one of the pilgrim visitors in Jerusalem for the feast hears his own home-language. One of the Twelve stands up with the Eleven to preach to the whole crowd. Source: Acts 1–2 KJV.

stephen-the-first-martyr-and-the-young-m.context_blurb: In the early Jerusalem church, the apostles are overwhelmed and pick seven men to handle the daily food-distribution to the widows so that they themselves can keep preaching. Acts 6 names the very first of these seven — a man 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost' — and the long speech he gives before the Sanhedrin in Acts 7 is the longest in the book. His execution follows at once, and a young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus is standing nearby holding the coats of the men who throw the stones. Source: Acts 6–7 KJV.

peter-and-john-at-the-beautiful-gate-sil.context_blurb: In the book of Acts chapter 3, two of Jesus's apostles walk up together to the Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer, as they did every day. A man who has been lame since birth is laid daily at the gate called Beautiful to ask alms of the people going in. The two apostles stop, Peter speaks a famous line about silver and gold, and the man rises and goes into the Temple leaping and praising God. The Sanhedrin then arrests them for the night. Source: Acts 3 KJV.

the-damascus-road-the-light-the-voice-an.context_blurb: Before he was the apostle Paul, Saul of Tarsus was on the road hunting Christians. He carried official letters from the high priest in Jerusalem authorising him to arrest any followers of Jesus he could find in the synagogues of a particular city and drag them back in chains. On the way a sudden light from heaven knocked him to the ground and a voice spoke. The scene is told three times in Acts and remembered forever as the pattern of a sudden conversion. Sources: Acts 9, 22, 26 KJV.

the-jerusalem-council-and-the-split-of-p.context_blurb: At Antioch some men who had come down from Judea began teaching the Gentile converts that they could not be saved unless they also kept the full Law of Moses. The dispute was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas were sent down to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders. Acts 15 tells of the great council that followed and the letter the Jerusalem leaders sent back out to the Gentile churches. The same chapter ends with a sharp quarrel between Paul and Barnabas over whether to take John Mark along on a second journey. Source: Acts 15 KJV.

paul-at-the-areopagus-the-altar-to-the-u.context_blurb: Paul reaches Athens alone, waiting for Silas and Timothy to catch up. He walks the streets of the city, and one sight above all others stirs him up — the countless altars and statues on every corner. He is invited to speak at the Areopagus, the open-air court on a rocky hill below the Acropolis, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers are curious about his teaching. He opens from an altar he had seen in the city and quotes a line from the Cretan poet Epimenides. Source: Acts 17:16–34 KJV.

paul-and-silas-midnight-singing-the-phil.context_blurb: In the Macedonian city of Philippi, a slave girl follows the apostle Paul and his companion Silas through the streets for days, shouting after them. She is possessed by a particular kind of spirit, and when Paul finally commands it out of her, her owners drag the two missionaries into the market-square. By nightfall Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, locked in the inner prison with their feet in the stocks — and singing hymns at midnight. An earthquake opens every door. Source: Acts 16 KJV.

paul-before-agrippa-and-festus-almost-th.context_blurb: After his arrest in the Temple at Jerusalem, Paul is held for two years in Roman custody at the Mediterranean port that served as the governor's headquarters in Judea. His case passes from one Roman governor to another and finally comes before the local Jewish king Herod Agrippa II and his sister Berenice. Paul tells his conversion-story for the third time in Acts, and Agrippa gives the famous half-answer that has become a proverb. Source: Acts 24–26 KJV.

shipwreck-on-malta-the-alexandrian-grain.context_blurb: In the autumn of about 60 CE Paul, still a prisoner, is being shipped from Caesarea to Rome under a Roman centurion named Julius. While the ship is at Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete, Paul warns against sailing on so late in the season. The centurion overrules him, a storm catches the ship, and the fourteen-day drift ends in shipwreck on a small Mediterranean island. The whole party reaches shore alive. The island's chief Publius takes them in. Source: Acts 27–28 KJV.

paul-beheaded-on-the-ostian-way.context_blurb: The book of Acts ends with Paul in Rome under a light form of house arrest, in his own rented house, receiving all who came and preaching freely. Acts does not describe his death. Later Christian tradition — Tertullian, Eusebius, and the Liber Pontificalis — places it under the emperor Nero and executes him by the sword rather than by the cross because of his Roman citizenship. His tomb is now covered by the great Roman basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls on the Ostian Way, and his feast is kept the same day as Peter's. Source: Acts 28; Tertullian, De Praescriptione.

john-on-patmos-the-four-horsemen-and-the.context_blurb: At the end of the first century, by Christian tradition, the aged apostle John was exiled by the Roman emperor Domitian to a small rocky island in the eastern Aegean for refusing to burn incense to the emperor. There he wrote down a long series of visions that became the last book of the Bible. The seven churches of Asia Minor, the four riders on four coloured horses, the woman clothed with the sun fleeing a great red dragon, and the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven are all in that book. Source: Revelation 1–21 KJV.

peter-crucified-upside-down-at-rome.context_blurb: By the end of his life, Christian tradition places the fisherman apostle Peter far from Galilee, leading the small Christian community in Rome itself. His first epistle sends greetings from 'Babylon,' which early Christians read as a code-name for Rome. In the summer of 64 CE the emperor Nero burned Christians to clear his own blame for the great fire of Rome; by tradition Peter was martyred in that persecution on the Vatican hill in a particular posture he had asked for because he counted himself unworthy to die the same way as Jesus. In 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that the bones under the high altar of St Peter's were almost certainly his. Source: 1 Peter 5; Eusebius 2.

the-silversmiths-of-ephesus-and-the-riot.context_blurb: In the city of Ephesus the apostle Paul rents out a lecture hall and teaches in it daily for two full years. The whole province hears him. The silversmiths of Ephesus, who make a living casting silver souvenirs of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — see their business falling off and start a riot. For two hours the mob in the theater of Ephesus shouts the same line in Greek over and over, until the town clerk finally calms them. Source: Acts 19 KJV.

aphrodite-born-from-the-sea-foam.context_blurb: In Greek myth, Aphrodite is the goddess of love and beauty, born in Hesiod's Theogony from the foam of the sea off the shore of a southern Mediterranean island. The Romans later worshipped her under their own name as Venus. One bird above all others is sacred to her and flies through her stories and perches on the shoulders of her statues. Her son by the war-god, her Olympian husband, and her Renaissance birth-painting on a scallop shell by Botticelli all gather around her. Sources: Hesiod, Theogony; Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite.

apollo-at-delphi-the-python-and-the-pyth.context_blurb: In Greek myth Apollo is the bright Olympian of music, prophecy, archery, and the sun. He is born as one of a pair of twins — his twin sister Artemis is the archer-goddess of the wild woods, born the same day on a small floating Aegean island. In childhood he slays a great earth-serpent and takes over the oracle at Delphi, whose temple-stone would carry two short maxims that generations of Greeks learned by heart. His tragic love for a Thessalian nymph gives his victor's crown its leaves, and his year of herding cattle for a mortal king is one of the strangest stories in his cycle. Sources: Homeric Hymn to Apollo; Ovid, Metamorphoses.

arachne-the-weaver-challenging-athena.context_blurb: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 6, a young weaver of Lydia named Arachne is so skilled at the loom that she dares to boast her work can match Athena's — and refuses to admit she owes anything to the goddess who invented weaving. Athena appears disguised as an old woman, warns her, and then unmasks for a contest. The two weave side by side; Athena's tapestry shows one scene and Arachne's another. The ending is one of the harshest transformations in the whole book. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.

ares-reviled-the-war-god-the-gods-hate.context_blurb: On Olympus one god is known for the fury of the killing-field itself — not the strategy of it, but the joy of the slaughter — while Athena keeps the strategic craft of war. Homer's Iliad barely hides its contempt for him: Zeus himself tells him he is the most hateful of all the gods on Olympus. His two sons go into battle with him with names meaning 'Terror' and 'Fear.' In Iliad Book 5 the mortal hero Diomedes, with Athena's help, actually wounds him in the belly. Source: Homer, Iliad 5.

artemis-and-actaeon-torn-by-his-own-houn.context_blurb: In Greek myth, Apollo has a twin sister among the twelve Olympians — the virgin goddess of the hunt, the wild woodland, and the silver bow. She runs the mountain slopes with a band of nymphs and hunting dogs, and in her stories she punishes any mortal who crosses her. In one of the most famous of these stories, a young hunter stumbles upon her bathing in a hidden pool on a Boeotian mountainside, and she makes sure he will never speak of what he saw. Sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca.

athenas-birth-fully-armed-from-zeuss-hea.context_blurb: In Hesiod's Theogony, Zeus has already cast down his father Cronus and taken his throne. He takes Metis, goddess of wise counsel, as his first wife — and while Metis is pregnant, Gaia (earth) and Ouranos (sky) come to him with a warning: her next child, a son, is fated to overthrow his father just as Zeus had overthrown his own. Zeus's answer is drastic. The result is a very strange birth of one of the twelve Olympians, out of a splitting headache. Source: Hesiod, Theogony.

demeter-and-persephone-the-pomegranate-s.context_blurb: In Greek myth Demeter is the older sister of Zeus and one of the twelve Olympians, the great goddess of grain and the harvest. She has a single beloved daughter fathered by Zeus. When that daughter is stolen away to the underworld in a lonely meadow, Demeter's grief freezes the fields of the whole world — and that is the story the Greeks told to explain why the earth has winter. The long search by torchlight, the welcome at Eleusis, the bargain in the underworld over a certain fruit, and the founding of the great Eleusinian Mysteries all come from the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.

deucalion-and-pyrrha-stones-thrown-over-.context_blurb: In Greek myth, when Zeus decides to drown the wicked human race in a great flood, one mortal couple is warned in time to survive. They are the king of the region of Phthia in Thessaly and his wife, the daughter of Prometheus's brother Epimetheus and Pandora. They float through the flood in a wooden chest, land on a mountain in central Greece, and are told by an oracle to refill the earth by throwing stones over their shoulders. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 1.

dionysus-twice-born-the-pirates-the-maen.context_blurb: In ancient Greece Dionysus was the god of wild rites, madness, and the drink made from crushed fermented grapes. The Romans called him Bacchus. The youngest of the twelve Olympian gods, he was born twice — once from a mortal mother who could not survive seeing a god in his full glory, and once from his father Zeus's own body. His festivals gave the world the first theater. His revenge on a king of Thebes, the pirates who tried to kidnap him on a Mediterranean ship, and the Cretan princess he found abandoned on the island of Naxos are all his stories. Sources: Euripides, Bacchae; Homeric Hymn to Dionysus.

echo-and-narcissus-the-voice-and-the-poo.context_blurb: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 3, a talkative mountain nymph lives in the forests of Boeotia. The goddess Hera lays a curse on her for chattering on to hide Zeus's tricks: she can never speak first, only wait for someone else to talk and then repeat their last words back. Along comes a beautiful young hunter whom every other nymph has already tried and failed to charm. The whole story — his cruelty, the still pool, the goddess who hears a prayer, and the flower that still grows in Greek fields — unfolds from there. Source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.

hades-and-the-underworld-cerberus-styx-c.context_blurb: In Greek myth the youngest brother of Zeus and Poseidon won the land of the dead when the three divided the universe between them by lot. He lives in a shadowy palace underground. A grim old boatman waits on the far shore of a black river that encircles his kingdom; a three-headed hound guards its gate; and three judges sit in the fields of asphodel. The newly-dead carry a small bronze coin placed under their tongue at burial, and the greatest sinners each have their own eternal punishment. Sources: Hesiod, Theogony; Virgil, Aeneid 6.

hephaestus-thrown-from-olympus-the-thron.context_blurb: Every Olympian god has a specialty — Zeus rules, Poseidon storms, Apollo shoots the bow — and one Olympian runs the forge. He hammers out the thunderbolts of Zeus, the armor of heroes, and every impossible metal thing the other gods need. According to Homer and Hesiod he was born lame; his mother threw him down from Olympus into the sea; he was raised by two sea-goddesses in a cave for nine years; and in revenge he once sent a magical golden throne up to Olympus that trapped the goddess who sat in it. Sources: Homer, Iliad 1 and 18; Hesiod, Theogony.

hera-the-peacocks-hundred-eyes.context_blurb: Zeus is the king of the Olympian gods, and his sister — and also his wife — is queen beside him, the divine patron of marriage and the mother of Ares. Her stories are mostly stories of jealousy: of the mortal girls Zeus pursues, and of the children he fathers on them. In one of the most famous, Zeus turns a mortal lover into a white cow to hide her, and the queen of the gods asks for the cow as a gift and sets a hundred-eyed herdsman to guard it. The eyes end up as decoration on the tail of her sacred bird. Sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca.

hermes-the-newborn-stealing-apollos-catt.context_blurb: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, a nymph named Maia bears Zeus a son in a cave on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia. The newborn jumps out of his cradle the very same morning, invents a musical instrument from a tortoise-shell he finds on the hill, and then goes and steals the sacred cattle of his half-brother Apollo. His father Zeus has to come down and settle the quarrel. The baby grows up to be the messenger of the Olympian gods and the guide of souls to the underworld. Source: Homeric Hymn to Hermes.

marsyas-midas-and-the-asss-ears.context_blurb: In Greek myth, Athena invented the double-piped flute called the aulos but threw it away in disgust when she saw her own cheeks puffing out in a reflection on the water. A satyr named Marsyas picked it up and became so good on it he challenged Apollo himself to a music contest. The judges set the terms: whoever lost would be at the winner's absolute mercy. The outcome of that contest, and the related story of the Phrygian king Midas who judged a later music-match and got a strange reward for his ears, both come from Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 11.

pandora-and-the-jar-hope-alone-remaining.context_blurb: In Hesiod's Works and Days, Prometheus the wise Titan has stolen fire from heaven and given it to mortals. Zeus's revenge is to have the gods make the first mortal woman — Pandora — out of earth and water. He sends her down as a gift to Prometheus's younger brother. She comes carrying a jar (later mistranslated 'box') she is told never to open. The famous ending of the story turns on what is left inside the jar after everything else has flown out. Source: Hesiod, Works and Days.

poseidon-and-athena-the-olive-and-the-sp.context_blurb: In Greek myth, one Olympian is lord of the sea, of horses, and of earthquakes. His wife is the sea-nymph Amphitrite. In one famous contest he competes with Athena for the right to be the patron god of a new city in Attica. The two offer gifts to the local king and his council — he strikes the rock with his trident and she plants a tree — and the council then has to decide. The losing god is bitter about it for the rest of the city's history. Source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.

prometheus-fire-in-the-fennel-stalk-the-.context_blurb: In Hesiod's Theogony, Prometheus the Titan sides with Zeus against his own Titan brothers in the great war for heaven, and keeps his freedom after the Olympians win. He then plays a long double game as the friend of mortal men — tricking Zeus at a sacrifice at Mecone, and stealing fire from heaven and smuggling it to earth hidden in the hollow of a plant-stalk. Zeus's revenge is to have him chained to a crag in the Caucasus, where an eagle comes every day to eat his liver. Sources: Hesiod, Theogony and Works and Days; Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound.

sisyphus-cheating-death-chaining-thanato.context_blurb: In Book 6 of Homer's Iliad, Homer gives Sisyphus a nickname that fits the whole story to come: he was, Homer says flat out, the craftiest of mortals. He twice cheats Death itself — once by chaining up the god of death in a cupboard so that nobody on earth can die until Ares has to come free him, and once by tricking Hades's queen into letting him go back up to the living on a technicality. tantalus-ixion-the-danaids-the-underworl.context_blurb: In Greek myth there is a special wing of the underworld reserved for mortals who committed outrages the gods could not forgive. the-madness-of-ajax-slaughtering-sheep-f.context_blurb: After Achilles was killed at Troy, his god-forged armor was awarded by the Greek chieftains to the warrior who most deserved it. the-trojan-horse-odysseuss-stratagem-and.context_blurb: After ten years of siege the Greeks still could not break the walls of Troy, so one of their leaders proposed a trick to get inside without a battle: build an enormous hollow wooden horse, hide a picked band of warriors inside it, and sail the rest of the fleet out of sight behind the island of Tenedos. helen-and-paris-in-troy-the-muster-of-a-.context_blurb: When Menelaus, king of Sparta, comes home from a trip to Crete to find that his wife and much of his palace treasure are both gone — sailed east across the Aegean with a prince from Troy — he goes to the chieftains who had sworn years earlier, as her suitors, to defend her marriage. When he is old enough his mother leads him to a great boulder and tells him to lift it. Underneath are two tokens his absent father Aegeus, king of Athens, had left there years before. Theseus chooses the overland road around the Saronic Gulf — the hard way, through a string of famous roadside bandits he kills each by that bandit's own method. Source: Plutarch, Theseus 7–11.

theseus-ariadnes-thread-and-the-black-sa.context_blurb: The Minotaur lived inside a great maze at Knossos on Crete, so cunningly designed that anyone who went in could never find the way out again. King Minos of Crete had it built by his own household craftsman and demanded a yearly tribute of young men and women from Athens to feed to the beast. One year Theseus volunteered to go. He left Athens under black sails, with his father telling him to swap them for white sails on the return if he lived. Source: Plutarch, Theseus 15–22.

theseus-and-pirithous-stuck-to-the-chair.context_blurb: The two sworn friends Theseus and Pirithous thought themselves worthy of daughters of Zeus. First they set out to help Theseus win his chosen wife — a girl still a child, whom Theseus carried off and left with his mother Aethra in Attica. Then Pirithous proposed something bolder still: that they go together down into Hades and bring back the queen of the underworld. The two walked down through a cave at Cape Tainaron and were offered seats at Hades's table. Source: Apollodorus, Epitome 1.

andvaris-ring-the-cursed-gold-that-start.context_blurb: The opening act of the Norse Volsung Saga is a chain of small accidents that make a cursed treasure. Three Aesir gods — Odin, Honir, and the trickster — are walking across the world when the trickster kills a small brown river-animal at the foot of a waterfall. The animal turns out to be a wizard's shape-shifting son, and the dead son's family demands blood-money in gold enough to cover the pelt. The trickster is sent to find that much gold at any price, and the price turns out to include a magic ring and a curse. The whole family of the dead son, and the dwarf under the waterfall, drive the rest of the Volsung cycle. Source: Volsunga Saga ch. 14; Reginsmal.

angrbodas-children-fenrir-jormungandr-an.context_blurb: In Snorri Sturluson's thirteenth-century Prose Edda, three terrible children of Loki come into the world together by a giantess he keeps as a secret lover in Jotunheim. One is a wolf raised among the gods until he outgrows them. One is a serpent cast into the sea around the world of men. One is a girl given rule over the dreary underworld of those who die of sickness and old age — her hall and its servants have grim punning names, which Snorri inventories one by one in chapter 34 of his Gylfaginning. All three children are released again at Ragnarok. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning 34.

baldrs-death-mistletoe-hodr-and-the-gian.context_blurb: In Snorri Sturluson's thirteenth-century Prose Edda, the best-loved of all the Norse Aesir is a young man so fair and gentle that light itself shines from him — the son of Odin the All-Father and the goddess Frigg. He begins having terrible dreams that keep waking him, and the mother-goddess walks through every one of the nine worlds trying to protect him. The story of what happens to this gentle god, the god who tries to bring him back from the underworld, and the one old woman who refuses to weep for him is told fullest in Snorri's Gylfaginning and the Eddic poem Baldrs draumar.

beowulf-tears-off-grendels-arm.context_blurb: In the Old English poem Beowulf, written down in Anglo-Saxon England around the year 1000 but set in older heroic Scandinavia, a young Geat hero sails to Denmark to help King Hrothgar. A monster descended from Cain has raided the Danish mead-hall Heorot every night for twelve years. Beowulf and his fourteen thanes settle in to wait for the monster, and Beowulf makes a striking choice about how he will meet it. The whole poem has come down to us across a thousand years through a single lucky manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, which was nearly destroyed by fire in London in 1731. Source: Beowulf.

brynhild-in-the-ring-of-fire.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsung Saga, the young hero Sigurd — fresh from killing the dragon Fafnir and the smith Regin — rides his horse Grani along a road the birds have pointed him to, up a great mountain. From miles off he sees the mountain's crown ringed with a blaze of flame so tall that no bird flies through it. The woman he finds on the mountain, in a long helmet-coat, is the woman the whole rest of the saga will turn on; Richard Wagner later built the climax of his great Ring opera cycle on her. The one gathering of pages missing from the Codex Regius is in this part of the story. Source: Volsunga Saga; Wagner, Ring.

brynhilds-revenge-guttorm-kills-sigurd-i.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsung cycle Sigurd is married to Gudrun; her brother Gunnar is married to Brynhild, who still believes it was Gunnar who crossed the ring of fire to wake her. One morning the two queens go to a river to wash their hair, and there they quarrel. From that quarrel the saga winds steadily down into blood: a demand for Sigurd's death, a hunt in the forest, a sword-blow in a certain place, and a funeral pyre on which more than one body burns. Richard Wagner built the ending of his great Ring opera cycle on the same material. Sources: Volsunga Saga; Reginsmal; Wagner, Gotterdammerung.

draupnir-odins-ring-that-drips-eight-mor.context_blurb: The magical gold arm-ring worn by the chief of the Norse gods earns its name from what it does over and over — gold falls off it in fresh rings like drops of water off a wet blade. The Old Norse name simply means 'the dripper.' The ring belongs to the cluster of famous named objects in Norse myth that the dwarves forged in the smithing-contest of the six treasures. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Skaldskaparmal.

fimbulwinter-three-winters-with-no-summe.context_blurb: In Norse mythology, the world does not end quietly. Almost every named Aesir god dies in one great final battle, the sky splits, and the sea rises to swallow the earth. The Voluspa poem of the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda both describe the long run-up — a great winter with no summer between, a wolf-age of men who kill their own kin, and a specific wolf that at last catches and swallows the sun it has been chasing across the sky. Sources: Voluspa; Snorri's Gylfaginning.

freyja-cats-falcon-cloak-and-the-brising.context_blurb: In Norse myth the goddess Freyja of the Vanir came to live in Asgard after the war between the Aesir and the Vanir. She is the great goddess of love and gold, half-sister of Freyr, and her chariot is pulled by two great animals of a kind no other god drives. She owns a falcon-cloak that any god may borrow to fly in. The story of how she bought her signature necklace from four dwarves is one of the strangest in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Lokasenna.

freyr-the-sword-he-traded-for-love.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the god of sunshine, good weather, harvest, and peace is not one of the Aesir by birth. He belongs to the older tribe of gods — the Vanir — who were traded to the Aesir as hostages after their war. His greatest treasure is a magic sword that fights by itself. But in the poem Skirnismal he climbs onto Odin's seat Hlidskjalf and sees a giantess he cannot stop thinking about, and sends his servant Skirnir to woo her for him. The price he pays for her comes due at Ragnarok. Source: Skirnismal; Snorri's Prose Edda.

gleipnir-and-tyrs-hand-the-six-impossibl.context_blurb: In the Norse stories Loki has three monstrous children by the giantess Angrboda — the death-goddess Hel, a great serpent that will grow long enough to circle the whole world, and a third child that terrifies the Aesir most of all. The gods try to bind him twice with iron fetters named Leyding and Dromi, and both snap. The dwarves of Svartalfheim make them a third binding out of six things that do not exist — a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the breath of fish, and three more — and one god is willing to prove his good faith to the wolf by laying his hand in its jaws. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

gram-in-the-barnstokk-the-sword-only-sig.context_blurb: In the middle of King Volsung's great hall stands a living oak the family call Barnstokk — 'child-trunk' — with its branches spreading up through the roof-beams. On the night of Signy's wedding-feast a one-eyed stranger walks in and does one shocking thing to the tree before he leaves. Every warrior in the hall tries to pull his sword from the trunk, and only Sigmund — one of the youngest men there — can draw it out. The whole Volsung dynasty will carry the pieces of that sword forward. Source: Volsunga Saga ch. 3.

grendels-mother-in-the-mere-the-giant-sw.context_blurb: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has torn off the arm of a monster named Grendel and hung it in the rafters of the mead-hall Heorot as a trophy. That same night a second monster comes to Heorot for revenge — Grendel's mother. Beowulf tracks her to her cave beneath a dark lake, and the fight at the bottom turns on a weapon not in his pack. Later tradition and the poem itself call his band of thanes 'the Geats.' Source: Beowulf.

grimhilds-potion-and-the-ride-through-th.context_blurb: The old king Gjuki of the Rhine has a queen who is far more dangerous than he is: a powerful sorceress who knows how to brew charmed drinks and speaks spells over them. She will engineer every disaster in the second half of the Volsunga Saga — a potion of forgetting handed to the hero, a swap of faces that lets another man cross the ring of fire in his shape, and the brothering oath that leads to Sigurd's murder in his own bed. Source: Volsunga Saga.

gullinbursti-the-golden-boar-that-lights.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the harvest-and-sunshine god of the Vanir owns a chariot pulled by a shining animal forged of solid gold. The dwarves Sindri and Brokkr made it in the great smithing-contest that produced the six treasures. Its name comes from its golden bristles, and it can swim through sea and run through air faster than any horse. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Skaldskaparmal.

gungnir-odins-spear-that-never-misses.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the All-Father Odin, chief of the Aesir and lord of the slain in Valhalla, carries a signature weapon into every battle — the same weapon he takes with him on his last ride out at Ragnarok. The dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi forged it. It is also what Odin leaned on during his nine days hanging from the world-tree for the runes. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Havamal.

heimdallr-blows-the-gjallarhorn.context_blurb: In the Norse myths a shining god stands on the arch of the rainbow that joins the world of humans to the world of the gods. His whole duty is to watch: no giant may cross without his seeing it first. He drinks only pure mead, his hearing is so sharp he can hear grass growing on the earth, and when at last Ragnarok comes he lifts his great horn and blows a blast that every realm of the nine worlds hears. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

heimdallr-gjallarhorn-and-grass-growing.context_blurb: A rainbow bridge stretches from the world of humans up to the home of the gods. One god stands guard at its far end and lets no giant across. He sleeps less than a bird, sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day, and keeps his horn by him for the day of the last battle. In another old poem Rigsthula he walks among mortals under a different name and fathers the three classes of men. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Rigsthula.

heorot-the-hall-where-grendel-comes-at-n.context_blurb: The greatest surviving poem in the Old English language tells of a young warrior who sails across the sea to kill a hall-monster and, decades later, dies fighting a dragon. The whole first half is set in the mead-hall King Hrothgar built in Denmark, where the monster has haunted the night for twelve years. The poem itself survives in a single eleventh-century manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, from the British Library. Source: Beowulf.

hrungnir-the-whetstone-in-thors-forehead.context_blurb: In Snorri Sturluson's Skaldskaparmal, the strongest of all the giants has a stone heart, a stone head, a stone shield — his whole body is made of rock. He challenges Thor to single combat at a place called Griotunagard, and the giants build him a companion out of clay nine leagues tall to stand beside him. The duel ends with a whetstone lodged in Thor's forehead that a volva — the seeress Groa — later tries to chant out. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

huginn-and-muninn-thought-and-memory.context_blurb: Odin sits on his high seat in Asgard, but he cannot be in every corner of the world at once. To keep watch on all of Midgard he sends out two of the same kind of bird every dawn to fly the whole earth and come back at breakfast. Their names mean Thought and Memory. He also has two wolves named Geri and Freki beside his throne who eat his meat for him. He himself takes only wine. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Grimnismal.

idunns-apples-loki-the-eagle-and-the-kid.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the Aesir stay young because one goddess of Asgard keeps a wooden box of golden fruit and hands them around at every feast. The gods eat from her box; without it they would age like any mortal. In the story Snorri tells in Skaldskaparmal, Loki accidentally leads the giant Thjazi, in the shape of an eagle, straight into her garden — and then has to turn around and get her back. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

kvasir-and-the-mead-of-poetry-dwarves-bl.context_blurb: In the Norse origin of poetry itself, the two families of gods — the Aesir and the Vanir — ended their long war by sealing peace in one shared act at a great vat. Every god spat into it, and out of that spit grew a man named Kvasir, the wisest being alive. Two dwarves killed him and brewed his blood with honey into a magical mead that gave the gift of poetry to anyone who drank it. The giant Suttung took the mead for himself, and Odin went on a long trip to steal it back. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

lokasenna-the-flyting-at-aegirs-feast.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, one of the great banquet-hosts of the Aesir and Vanir is a sea-figure who brews ale in an enormous cauldron under the waves and invites the gods down to drink. The poem Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda sets Loki at that feast — hurling an insult at every god in turn and daring any of them to answer. Thor's final arrival ends the party. The sea-host's servants are also part of the story. Source: Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda.

lokis-brood-in-the-norse-imagination-kin.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the trickster Loki lives among the Aesir gods in Asgard, but Snorri opens his genealogy in the Prose Edda by pointing out that Loki is not one of the Aesir by blood at all. He is Odin's sworn brother, and that oath is what keeps him in Asgard. He has a loyal goddess wife named Sigyn and two sons by her; he also has three monstrous children by a giantess in Jotunheim; and once, as a mare, he mothered Odin's own eight-legged horse. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

lokis-lips-sewn-shut-the-head-forfeit-do.context_blurb: In Snorri's smithing-contest of the six treasures, two dwarf-brothers named Brokkr and Sindri compete against the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi for Loki's head. When the gods judge which of the six treasures is finest, the winning object goes to Thor — the war-hammer he will carry into every battle for the rest of Norse story. Loki tries to wriggle out of the wager on a technicality: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck. Brokkr's answer, with his brother's awl, is one of the ugliest moments in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

lokis-punishment-bound-with-naris-entrai.context_blurb: Loki flees the wrath of the gods after the death of Baldr and hides in the mountains. He builds himself a paranoid house with one door on each of its four sides so that he can see every direction at once, and he turns into a salmon by day to swim in a waterfall. The gods catch him at last with a fishing-net he himself had just invented. His punishment is one of the darkest scenes in Norse myth — his loyal wife Sigyn sits with him in a cave with a wooden bowl, catching the venom that drips from a serpent fastened above him, until Ragnarok comes. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

mjolnir-the-hammer-of-thor.context_blurb: In Norse myth the red-bearded god of thunder rides across the sky in a chariot pulled by two goats, and the flash of his signature weapon is what people down in Midgard see as lightning. The dwarves Sindri and Brokkr forged it. It never misses what Thor throws it at, always returns to his hand, and the gods raise it to consecrate every funeral pyre. The small silver hammer-pendants hung around Viking necks have survived in great numbers. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda.

mjolnir-the-hammer-with-the-too-short-ha.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god carries a single signature weapon that the Aesir gods count on above every other blade in Asgard when the giants of Jotunheim come down from the mountains. In the smithing-contest in which the dwarves Sindri and Brokkr forged it, Loki as a fly bit the dwarf's eye at a crucial moment — and the shortness of the hammer's handle was the result. Thor still kills the Midgard Serpent with it at Ragnarok. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal; Gylfaginning.

naglfar-the-ship-of-dead-mens-nails.context_blurb: In the Norse story of Ragnarok, the sea rises up over Midgard, the wolf Fenrir breaks loose, and a great ship sails out of the east across the flooded world, carrying an army of giants and monsters to the last battle. What that ship is made of is one of Snorri's grimmest details — and Snorri uses it to urge every Norseman to groom the dead before burial so as to delay the ship's finishing just a little longer. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.
