odin-against-fenrir-vidarrs-shoe-and-the.context_blurb: In the Norse story of the last battle, a monstrous wolf breaks loose after ages of being bound, and races across the world to devour the All-Father himself. Odin's silent son Vidarr is the one who finally answers him. Vidarr wears a huge boot of leather scraps trimmed from every boot ever made in Midgard — Snorri tells craftsmen to throw away such trimmings so Vidarr's shoe will be large enough. The scene at Ragnarok that follows is one of the most-painted in Norse mythology. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Vafthrudnismal.

odin-at-mimirs-well-trading-an-eye-for-a.context_blurb: The chief god of the Aesir in Norse myth is called the All-Father — lord of Asgard, master of poetry, war, and death. He is the father of Thor and the husband of Frigg. In Snorri's Prose Edda he once walks to the roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil, where a severed head keeps watch over a well of wisdom, and asks for a drink. The price the head demands is high. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

odin-on-yggdrasil-nine-nights-for-the-ru.context_blurb: Odin has already paid one eye at Mimir's well for a taste of wisdom, but he is still hungry for a deeper knowledge — the magical marks that shape fate itself, the ones gods and men still carve on stone and wood. In the poem Havamal of the Poetic Edda, he describes hanging on a windy tree, pierced by his own spear, given to himself, no bread, no drinking-horn, for nine nights. At the end of the ninth night he catches sight of what he came for and takes it screaming. Source: Havamal 138–145.

odin-the-wanderer-the-wild-hunt.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, one of the gods is often described walking the roads of Midgard disguised as an old man in a broad hat pulled down low, a grey-blue cloak, and a walking staff. He has only one eye, having traded the other long ago for a drink from Mimir's well. He rides an eight-legged horse that carries him between all the worlds. In Scandinavian folklore he still leads a shadowy band of hunters across the winter sky, a procession called the Oskoreia. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; folklore.

regin-reforges-the-sword-gram-from-shard.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga an old king dies in battle when his sword shatters against a stranger's spear — and he tells his young wife to keep the pieces for their unborn son. Years later that son grows up a foster-son of a cunning smith named Regin. Regin forges and reforges a sword from the shards, and the hero tests it by cleaving a block of iron down to its foundations. The whole arc behind the Volsung story also lies behind J. R. R. Tolkien's reforged sword in The Lord of the Rings. Source: Volsunga Saga.

sifs-golden-hair-the-prank-that-starts-t.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god has a wife who lives with him in Asgard and is famous among the gods for one particular beauty. Poets say no woman in the nine worlds has ever had hair like hers — long and thick and golden, falling all the way to the ground. One day Loki, playing a cruel joke, cuts it all off in her sleep. The scene is the opening prank that triggers the whole smithing-contest among the dwarves — and the six great Norse treasures. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

sigurd-slays-fafnir-the-pit-and-the-upwa.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga a young hero armed with his reforged father-sword Gram is sent by his foster-father Regin to kill a dragon coiled around a cursed hoard of gold on the moor called Gnitaheid. Regin tells him to dig a pit in the trail where the dragon slithers down to drink, and stab upward as the dragon passes over. Odin, meeting Sigurd in the shape of an old man, tells him to dig extra pits beside it to catch the poisonous blood. Source: Volsunga Saga; Fafnismal.

sigurd-tastes-the-dragons-blood-the-bird.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga the young hero has just killed the dragon on Gnitaheid. His foster-father Regin sits down beside him, cuts one specific organ out of the dragon, and hands it to the boy with orders to cook it over the open fire while Regin lies down to sleep in the grass. When the hero burns a thumb on the roasting meat and sucks it, he suddenly understands the speech of birds — and the birds are talking about Regin. Source: Volsunga Saga; Fafnismal.

skidbladnir-the-ship-that-folds-into-a-p.context_blurb: Among the Norse gods, one of the Vanir who came to live in Asgard is the god of harvest, sunshine, and good weather — the god the farmers of Sweden and Norway prayed to for a peaceful year and a good crop. He owns a golden boar and a magic ship. The ship, forged by the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi, holds all the gods of Asgard together, always has a fair wind, and folds up small enough to carry in a pouch. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

sleipnir-loki-as-a-mare-and-odins-eight-.context_blurb: In Norse myth Odin the All-Father rides a great grey horse that can carry him between all the worlds, even down into the land of the dead. Snorri says this horse is stranger than any other horse ever born because of one feature of its body. The story of how it came to be — a bargain the Aesir made with a master builder for the walls of Asgard, and Loki's transformation into a mare — is told in Snorri's Gylfaginning. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Hyndluljod.

surtr-the-fire-giant-with-the-flaming-sw.context_blurb: In the Norse cosmos hung on the branches of the world-tree Yggdrasil, one of the nine worlds sits at the far southern edge, older than Asgard and older than the gods themselves — one of two primal worlds that existed before creation. A fire-giant stands at its border with a flaming sword, and at Ragnarok he leads the giants out against the gods and sets the whole universe on fire. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

the-master-builder-the-walls-of-asgard-f.context_blurb: In the Prose Edda a stranger arrives at the hall of the Norse gods and offers to build them a great stone rampart — one no giant will ever be able to break through. The gods ask his price, and the price turns out to be unthinkable. Loki promises he can get the wall built without the gods having to pay. The stranger has a stallion named Svadilfari who hauls stones for him, and Loki solves the problem with another transformation. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

the-norns-at-the-well-of-urd.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the whole cosmos hangs from one great tree with three roots — one reaching to the frost-giants, one to Hel, and one to the gods. Under a hall by a well at the gods' root live three fate-women who choose the life of every mortal and god. They carve runes on a stave of ash, water the roots of the tree with milk-coloured water, and keep the whole cosmos from rotting away. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

the-three-roosters-gullinkambi-fjalar-an.context_blurb: In the Voluspa of the Poetic Edda three roosters crow at the dawn of Ragnarok. One crows in Jotunheim to wake the giants, one crows in Asgard to wake the Aesir, and one crows down in Hel to wake the dead. The three birds between them wake up the whole universe for the last battle. Source: Voluspa.

the-wager-loki-bets-his-head-with-brokkr.context_blurb: In the Prose Edda Loki once cut off the golden hair of Thor's wife as a prank, and to save his own life he went down to the dwarf-quarter to have new hair made. His habit of bragging landed him in a much bigger scrape while he was there. He wagered against two more dwarves, Brokkr and Sindri, that they could not make three gifts to equal the three the first dwarves had already made for the gods. The three judges of the contest were the three heads of the Aesir pantheon. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

thor-and-jormungandr-fishing-with-hymir.context_blurb: The Norse Midgard Serpent is the great sea-monster that wraps the whole world — so long he holds his own tail in his teeth. He is one of three monstrous children Loki fathered on the giantess Angrboda; his two siblings are Hel the death-goddess and Fenrir the wolf. The story of how Thor once nearly caught him on a fishing trip with the giant Hymir, with an ox-head as bait, is one of the strangest in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Hymiskvida.

thor-and-jormungandr-nine-paces-from-the.context_blurb: Thor the thunder-god has met the world-serpent Jormungandr twice before their final meeting at Ragnarok, and both times the fight ends without a winner. The first time is at the hall of the giant-king Utgard-Loki, where Thor is challenged to lift a huge grey cat off the floor — but the cat is really the world-serpent in disguise. At Ragnarok the two of them finally face each other in the open on the plain of Vigrid. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thor-at-utgardaloki-the-horn-the-cat-and.context_blurb: On the first night of his journey east Thor and his companions find what looks like a huge empty hall and crawl inside to sleep. At dawn they realise the 'hall' was actually part of a giant's clothing dropped on the road. The whole trip is one humiliation after another — a drinking-horn he cannot drain, a cat he cannot lift, an old woman he cannot wrestle to the ground. Only at the end does their host Utgard-Loki reveal what each of those contests really was. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thors-goats-eaten-at-supper-alive-at-daw.context_blurb: In the Norse stories one god does not ride a horse at all. He crosses the sky in a chariot pulled by two goats whose hooves strike sparks against the clouds. At supper on a journey he slaughters and roasts the goats and shares the meat with whichever household he is lodging in — and in the morning he raises them again with his hammer. The bones must all go back onto the hide whole. On one such night a peasant's son cannot resist marrow in a bone — and the goat limps the next morning. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thors-wedding-veil-recovering-mjolnir-fr.context_blurb: In the Norse poem Thrymskvida, the thunder-god of the Aesir wakes one morning, gropes for the weapon he has always kept beside him, and finds only empty air. He shakes his beard so hard in fury that all Asgard hears it, and calls at once for Loki. Freyja refuses to be married off to the giant Thrym to get the weapon back — so Thor is dressed up as the bride instead, and the wedding feast at the giant's hall is one of the funniest scenes in Norse poetry. Source: Thrymskvida.

tyr-and-garmr-loki-and-heimdallr-the-mut.context_blurb: In the Norse binding of the wolf Fenrir, one god steps forward and lays his hand in the wolf's jaws as a pledge of good faith, and loses it when the trick is sprung. The same god gives his name to the Tuesday of the week in English and most Germanic languages. At Ragnarok he kills and is killed by the hound Garmr; nearby, Loki and Heimdallr are also mutually killed. Sources: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

wiglaf-at-the-dragon-only-one-man-stays.context_blurb: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has grown old. Fifty years after tearing off Grendel's arm in the Danish mead-hall Heorot, Beowulf has been king of the Geats for a long time, ruling in peace. Then trouble comes to his own land — a runaway slave stumbles into a barrow-mound on a headland and steals a golden cup. A dragon that had been sleeping on the hoard for three centuries wakes up and begins burning the countryside. Only one of his twelve chosen companions stays with him at the fight. Source: Beowulf.

the-world-rises-again-lif-and-lifthrasir.context_blurb: In Norse myth Ragnarok is the doom of the gods — Odin swallowed by the wolf, Thor down beside the world-serpent, Surt burning the whole world with fire, and the sea rising to cover every land. But the Voluspa, the great seeress-poem of the Poetic Edda, does not stop there. In stanza 59 the seeress sees something rise again, and names those who come out of a hidden grove to repopulate it — along with golden gaming pieces of the old gods found in the grass of the new fields. Source: Voluspa.

yggdrasil-the-world-tree-and-its-residen.context_blurb: At the centre of the Norse cosmos stands a single enormous tree whose branches spread above all the worlds and whose roots reach down to three separate wells. The Voluspa calls it 'a tall tree, showered with shining loam.' Four stags browse on its leaves, an eagle sits in its top, a dragon gnaws its deepest root, and a squirrel runs insults up and down the trunk between the eagle and the dragon. Source: Grimnismal; Voluspa; Snorri's Gylfaginning.

agatha-of-sicily-the-tongs-and-the-earth.context_blurb: Agatha was a young Christian woman killed for her faith in Sicily around the year 251, during one of the first great empire-wide persecutions of Christians. Her city still keeps her white silk veil in a shrine, and every February her feast is one of the biggest festivals on the island. The Passio Agathae and the Legenda Aurea tell her story in a long sequence of trials: a Roman emperor's empire-wide sacrifice edict, the local Roman governor's attempt to break her, and a night visitor to her prison cell after her worst torture. Her veil is still carried out of her shrine when Mount Etna threatens the villages below. Sources: Passio Agathae; Legenda Aurea.

agnes-of-rome-thirteen-years-old-on-the-.context_blurb: Agnes was a Christian girl in the city of Rome, only twelve or thirteen years old, at the beginning of the fourth century AD. She was rich, beautiful, and sought-after as a bride, but she had vowed herself to Christ and refused every suitor. During the great Diocletian persecution one of those rejected suitors denounced her to the Roman authorities, which set her story into motion. The earliest full narrative comes from Ambrose of Milan's De Virginibus around 377 CE. She was buried in a catacomb on the Via Nomentana. Sources: Ambrose, De Virginibus; Passio Agnetis.

ambrose-of-milan-acclaimed-bishop-before.context_blurb: In the year 374 the northern Italian city of Milan needed a new bishop. Ambrose, a Roman lawyer and the imperial governor of the province, had come to the city's church only to keep the peace during the election between rival factions. He was not yet a priest — in fact, he was not even baptized. What happened in the crowded church that day, and his frantic attempt to escape being made bishop, are told in Paulinus's Vita Ambrosii, which Paulinus wrote as Ambrose's own secretary. Ambrose eventually became one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Western Church.

anthony-of-the-desert-the-demons-and-pau.context_blurb: Around the year 270, a wealthy young Coptic Egyptian Christian named Anthony walked into a village church one Sunday and heard a gospel line that struck him as spoken for him alone. Within the week he had sold the family land, given the money away, and walked out into the desert for good. He lived to be over a hundred years old, and his biography — written by Athanasius of Alexandria around 360 CE — became the pattern for Christian monasticism in East and West. Jerome's Life of Paul of Thebes adds a famous story of the old Anthony crossing the deeper wilderness to visit an even older hermit. Sources: Athanasius, Vita Antonii; Jerome, Vita Pauli.

augustines-garden-tolle-lege.context_blurb: A young North African rhetorician was teaching in Milan in the mid-380s CE, listening to the sermons of its great bishop but unable to change how he lived. His Christian mother had followed him from Africa and kept praying for him. His Confessions tells the famous story of his conversion in a garden over an open copy of the letters of a New Testament apostle. His best friend, his son, and the enormous historical and philosophical defense of Christianity he later wrote against the fall of Rome all gather round the Confessions. Source: Augustine, Confessions.

benedict-of-nursia-the-raven-the-cup-and.context_blurb: In the late 400s a young Italian nobleman from Norcia in central Italy was sent to Rome to study and hated what he saw there. He walked out and lived alone as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco in the mountains east of Rome. Later he founded a great monastery at Monte Cassino and wrote a Rule of prayer and work that shaped Western monasticism for more than a thousand years. His twin sister Scholastica was also later remembered as a saint. Source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues Book 2.

blandina-at-lyon-the-slave-girl-and-the-.context_blurb: In 177 CE, during the Roman persecution of Christians in the Gallic city of Lugdunum (modern Lyon), a group of Christians was arrested and brought to the arena. The surviving Letter of the Churches of Lyon and Vienne — preserved in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History — names among them a young enslaved girl whose mistress feared she would break under torture. Instead the torturers, working on her in relays, finally admitted they were exhausted. The letter also names a boy of fifteen alongside her. Source: Letter preserved in Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica 5.1.

brigid-of-kildare-the-flame-the-butter-a.context_blurb: A young girl of the fifth century in Ireland keeps giving her father's food, cloaks, and cattle to the poor until he lets her take the veil. She grows up to found the most famous abbey of eastern Ireland, in a town whose old Irish name means 'church of the oak,' and becomes one of the three patron saints of the whole island alongside the great Welsh-born missionary and the Irish-born monk of Iona. Her community kept a sacred fire tended in turns by her holy nuns. Source: Cogitosus, Vita Sanctae Brigidae.

cecilia-of-rome-three-strokes-and-the-si.context_blurb: In the Roman church's old tradition, Cecilia was a young Roman noblewoman of the third century who was married against her wish to a pagan husband and won him for Christ on their wedding night. Her story grew into one of the great martyr-legends of Rome — her slow death in her own home, her burial in the catacomb of Callixtus, and the Roman church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere where she is still kept. Centuries later she became the patroness of music, and Chaucer picked up her story in the Canterbury Tales and gave it to one of his pilgrims to tell on the road. Sources: Passio Caeciliae; Chaucer.

christopher-the-giant-at-the-river-and-t.context_blurb: In old Christian legend, a giant later baptized Christopher waded across a raging river with a small child on his shoulders, and only after reaching the far bank learned who the child really was. His Greek name is a compound of two words — the first is Christos, meaning Christ. The medieval Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine tells the full story, including the big man's original pagan name before his conversion. Source: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea.

columba-of-iona-the-psalter-the-battle-a.context_blurb: An Irish monk of royal blood, born around 521 CE and trained as a scribe under Finnian at Movilla, later sailed off to the west of Scotland and founded the most famous island monastery of the Atlantic world on a small island of the Inner Hebrides. His biographer Adomnan tells how a copyright dispute in Ireland sent him into exile, how he faced down a water-monster in the Highland loch of Ness, and how his monks at Iona kept running one of the great manuscript workshops of early medieval Europe. Sources: Adomnan, Vita Columbae.

genevieve-of-paris-prayer-against-attila.context_blurb: Genevieve is born around the year 420 in a village a few miles west of the Roman town of Lutetia — the old Latin name for the city that would become one of the great capitals of Europe and whose patron saint she still is. In 451, when the Hunnic armies swept across Gaul, she called the city's women to prayer rather than flight, and the Huns swerved past. Decades later, when a different conquering army did arrive, she negotiated with its king. Her burial-place later became a famous Roman-style domed monument in the Latin Quarter. Source: Vita Genovefae.

george-and-the-dragon-of-silene.context_blurb: The historical George whom the medieval world made into its most famous dragon-slaying knight was in real life a Christian soldier of the Roman army, executed on 23 April 303 CE at Lydda in Palestine. His dragon-fight is a later story, added by the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine in the thirteenth century — a Libyan city threatened by a dragon in its lake, a princess sent out as a sacrifice, and a knight who tames the dragon with a girdle. George became the patron saint of England by vow of King Edward III. Source: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea.

ignatius-of-antioch-the-wheat-of-god.context_blurb: Around 108 CE a Christian bishop was arrested in the Syrian capital under the emperor Trajan and sentenced to be sent to the arena in Rome. He spent the last months of his life walking under guard across Anatolia to his execution, writing seven letters to the churches along the way (and one to Bishop Polycarp of Smyrna) that are among the earliest surviving Christian writings outside the New Testament. His chain-gang of ten Roman soldiers he nicknamed 'leopards.' Source: Letters of Ignatius; Eusebius.

jerome-the-lion-and-the-vulgate.context_blurb: In a cave-cell in Bethlehem, an old scholar named Jerome bent over his lamp-lit desk for the last thirty-four years of his life, working on one enormous project at the request of Pope Damasus: a single Latin Bible for all of Western Europe. He had learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers in Palestine so he could translate the Old Testament straight from the original. The medieval legend adds a lion who turned up at his monastery with a thorn in its paw and became his companion. Source: Jerome's letters; Golden Legend.

lawrence-of-rome-the-gridiron-and-the-tr.context_blurb: In 258 CE, during the brief but severe persecution under the Roman emperor Valerian, Pope Sixtus II was arrested and executed. Three days later the same emperor's officials came for the pope's chief deacon in Rome, who held the role of archdeacon and was in charge of the Roman church's silver plate, its register of help to the widows and poor, and all of its daily charity. He was ordered to hand over the church's treasure. The way he answered that order became one of the most famous moments of early Christian defiance. Source: Prudentius, Peristephanon 2.

martin-of-tours-half-a-cloak-at-the-gate.context_blurb: One bitter winter night on the road into a city in northern Gaul, a young Roman cavalry officer named Martin — a native of Pannonia on the Danube — came upon a beggar shivering nearly naked in the freezing wind. He had no money and nothing to give, so he drew his sword, cut his own cloak in half, and handed one piece to the beggar. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak. The rest of his life — his refusal to fight before the battle of Worms, the founding of his monastery at Marmoutier, his bishopric of Tours — is told in Sulpicius Severus's Vita Martini. Source: Sulpicius Severus, Vita Martini.

nicholas-of-myra-three-bags-through-the-.context_blurb: Nicholas was a fourth-century bishop of Myra in Asia Minor who became the most beloved popular saint of the Christian world. One of his most famous legends tells how, when he learned of three sisters whose impoverished father could not afford dowries and was about to sell them, he threw three bags of gold through their window at night to save them. In the medieval Netherlands and across northern Europe his December feast grew into a long tradition that eventually gave the modern world Santa Claus. Source: Vita Nicolai; Dutch folklore.

patrick-of-ireland-six-years-a-shepherd-.context_blurb: The patron saint of Ireland, whose feast fills the streets of Dublin, Boston, and New York every 17 March, was born around 385 CE into a Roman-Christian family in Roman Britain. His father Calpurnius was a local Roman magistrate and his grandfather had been a priest. At about sixteen he was kidnapped by Irish raiders and spent six years as a shepherd-slave in Ireland before escaping. Years later he came back as a bishop. His own words in his Confessio open with a famous one-line self-description. Source: Patrick, Confessio.

perpetua-and-felicity-the-ladder-and-the.context_blurb: In the year 203 CE, during the persecution under the emperor Septimius Severus, a young noblewoman named Perpetua of Carthage was arrested with a group of fellow catechumens including an eight-months-pregnant enslaved woman named Felicity. Perpetua kept a diary in prison that survives — one of the earliest first-person documents by a Christian woman. The whole party was finally brought into the arena, which the two women faced side by side on the day of the games. Source: Passio Perpetuae et Felicitatis.

polycarp-of-smyrna-eighty-and-six-years.context_blurb: A very old Christian bishop was dragged out of a farmhouse outside Smyrna on the west coast of Asia Minor, an elderly disciple of the apostle John from the generation before. He was brought back to the city to face the Roman proconsul in the stadium. In the surviving letter of his church to the other Asian churches, his last words to the proconsul are preserved — a famous answer when he was asked to curse Christ. He is one of the earliest named martyrs after the apostles themselves. Source: Martyrdom of Polycarp.

sebastian-the-arrows-the-widow-and-the-c.context_blurb: A young officer in the emperor Diocletian's Praetorian Guard has been secretly visiting fellow soldiers in the cells to encourage them; he himself is a secret Christian, and he is denounced. Diocletian orders him executed. The famous image of his death — a young man tied to a post full of arrows — turns out, in the Legenda Aurea, not to be the end at all; a Roman widow named Lucina found him still alive and nursed him back to health. He was later martyred a second time. Source: Legenda Aurea.

simeon-stylites-thirty-seven-years-on-a-.context_blurb: A Syrian shepherd boy joined a monastery near Antioch in the fourth century, but his fasts and self-denial were so extreme that the other monks asked him to leave. He moved out to a stone hut alone — and then, trying to escape the crowds who still followed him, climbed up on top of a stone pillar and lived there for the rest of his life, raising the pillar higher as he went. The pillar's ruins at Qalat Simaan in Syria were a famous Christian pilgrimage site for centuries. Source: Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Religious History.

bede-the-venerable-at-jarrow-the-church-.context_blurb: Around the year 731 the monk Bede finished his greatest book, in five volumes, at the double monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria and dedicated it to the reigning Northumbrian king. The book is the Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum — the first great history of the English church and the single most important source for Anglo-Saxon England. Bede was a historian, a Bible-commentator, and the man who popularised the AD dating system for the Western world. He died with the Gospel of John on his desk. Source: Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica.

bernard-of-clairvaux-and-the-second-crus.context_blurb: Around 1113 a 22-year-old Burgundian nobleman talked about thirty of his own brothers, cousins, and friends into renouncing their careers and walking together into the struggling new reformed abbey of Citeaux in Burgundy, saving it from dying out. The young man went on to found a daughter-house in the valley of Wormwood, to write the first great Western commentaries on the Song of Songs, and in 1146 to preach the Second Crusade across Europe. He is one of the most influential monks of the entire Middle Ages. Source: Bernard, Sermons on the Song of Songs; Vita Prima.

boniface-felling-the-donar-oak-at-fritzl.context_blurb: In the early eighth century an English monk, born Winfrid in Devon, crossed the Rhine to preach to the pagan Franks and Hessians, sent with a commission from Pope Gregory II. The pope gave him a new Latin name, and by that name he became the great missionary bishop of the Germans. In 723 he walked up to a sacred tree at Geismar in Hesse dedicated to the Germanic thunder-god Donar and took an axe to it. He was finally killed by pagans at Dokkum in Frisia thirty years later. Source: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii.

catherine-of-siena-writing-to-popes.context_blurb: In 1347 in the Italian hill-town of Siena, a wool-dyer named Jacopo Benincasa and his wife Lapa had a baby daughter they named Caterina — Catherine. She was the youngest of twenty-five children. From early childhood Catherine was famous for seeing visions. She refused marriage, cut off her hair when her family tried to pressure her, and became one of the most influential mystics and political figures of fourteenth-century Europe. In 1376 she traveled down into France to confront a pope. Source: Raymond of Capua, Legenda Major.

charlemagne-and-alcuin-at-aachen-the-pal.context_blurb: In the year 800, in Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III came up behind the kneeling Frankish king during Mass, placed a crown on his head, and hailed him as Emperor of the Romans. Charlemagne (his biographer Einhard says) claimed he had not expected it. Einhard's little book paints Charlemagne in private — a huge man obsessed with learning who kept a wax tablet under his pillow all night and still never quite mastered reading and writing, and whose palace chapel at Aachen was modelled on San Vitale at Ravenna. His chief scholar at the palace school was the English monk Alcuin from York in Northumbria. Source: Einhard, Vita Caroli Magni.

clare-of-assisi-running-to-francis-in-th.context_blurb: In the Umbrian hill-town of Assisi in the early 1200s, a girl named Chiara Offreduccio — Clare — listened from an upstairs window while a strange young preacher named Francis, roughly twelve years older than she was, gathered crowds in the piazza below. On the night of Palm Sunday 1212 she slipped out of the house and ran down the hill through the fields to join him. Her community of 'Poor Clares' at San Damiano became the women's branch of the Franciscan movement. In 1240, with mercenary troops at Assisi's walls, she carried one sacred object out to meet them. Source: Legenda Sanctae Clarae.

cuthbert-of-lindisfarne-and-the-otters-w.context_blurb: As a young shepherd on the hills of Northumbria in 651, a boy named Cuthbert saw a vision in the night sky of angels carrying a soul to heaven. In the morning he learned that an Irish missionary had died at the same hour, and the boy decided to become a monk. His monastic life ended on the little tidal island of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast. When Viking raids began smashing the island in 793, the monks lifted his coffin and carried it with them for over a hundred years, hunting for a safe place to lay it down. Sources: Bede, Vita Cuthberti; the Historia de Sancto Cuthberto.

cyril-and-methodius-the-slavic-alphabet.context_blurb: Two Greek brothers from a Byzantine port in Thessalonica, where the Slavic language was widely heard on the streets, grew up to become the ninth-century missionaries who first put Slavic into writing. The elder was named Methodius; the younger took the monastic name by which the whole family is now remembered in Eastern and Slavic Christianity. In 867 the brothers stopped in Venice and defended their right to celebrate the liturgy in Slavic against the three-language theory of their opponents. Sources: Vita Cyrilli and Vita Methodii.

erasmus-the-humanist-the-prince-of-the-h.context_blurb: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was the leading Christian humanist of the early sixteenth century — a Dutch priest and classical scholar who travelled the courts of Europe. He wrote his most famous satire in about a week, as a guest at the London house of a good English friend; the Latin title is a joke on his host's own Latinised surname. His great scholarly achievement was a corrected Greek edition of the New Testament. His later debate with Martin Luther over the freedom of the will divided the humanist movement from the Reformation. Source: Erasmus, letters and works.

francis-of-assisi-stripping-naked-in-the.context_blurb: Francis of Assisi's father Pietro Bernardone made the family fortune not in banking or in war but in a single trade — one that took him regularly across the Alps to France for merchandise. The young Francis grew up a party-loving son of a cloth merchant, took part as a young man in a disastrous war with Perugia, and after a long illness and a famous moment at a ruined chapel outside the city, broke publicly with his father in the town square of Assisi. He went on to found the Franciscan movement. Source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima.

francis-the-stigmata-at-la-verna-and-the.context_blurb: On Christmas night 1223, in a hilltop village of the Rieti valley in central Italy, Francis of Assisi staged the first live Nativity scene — a real ox, a real ass, and a manger of straw, so the local peasants could picture the poverty of Bethlehem. Every crib and presepio since descends from that night. Two years later, up on Mount La Verna in Tuscany with his closest companion Brother Leo, Francis received five marks on his hands, feet, and side — the stigmata — the first recorded in Christian history. Source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Secunda; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior.

francis-the-wolf-of-gubbio-and-the-sermo.context_blurb: In the Umbrian hill-town of Gubbio, people were so afraid of a beast killing sheep and people outside the walls that they would only leave in armed bands. Francis walked out alone to meet it. The outcome of that meeting became one of the most beloved stories in the Little Flowers of Saint Francis. He is also remembered for addressing a flock of birds as his 'little sisters,' and for the Canticle of the Sun — one of the first great poems in the Italian vernacular, calling the sun, moon, water, and earth his brothers and sisters. Source: Fioretti; Legenda Maior.

francis-xavier-missionary-to-india-and-j.context_blurb: Francis Xavier was born in 1506 in the castle of Xavier, into a noble family of one of Europe's oldest peoples — neighbours of both France and Spain in the Pyrenees. In Paris he fell in with Ignatius of Loyola and became one of the first seven Jesuits. He sailed east as the first Jesuit missionary to India and later became the first Christian missionary to reach Japan. He died in sight of mainland China waiting for a boat. His right forearm, kept as a relic in Rome, is the only piece of him most Catholic pilgrims ever see. Source: Monumenta Xaveriana.

hildegard-of-bingen-visions-since-age-th.context_blurb: Hildegard of Bingen was a twelfth-century German Benedictine abbess, mystic, composer, scientist, and visionary. She later dictated to her secretary Volmar that she had been seeing visions of a brilliant light — 'a light so great my soul quaked' — since early childhood. Her illuminated book Scivias was approved by Pope Eugenius III at the Synod of Trier. She also wrote one of the first serious European works on natural medicine. Her 77 chants are still performed. Source: Hildegard, Scivias; Vita Sanctae Hildegardis.

ignatius-loyola-the-cannonball-at-pamplo.context_blurb: Inigo Lopez de Loyola — later Ignatius — was born in 1491 at his family's castle in the mountainous northern region of Spain, where he grew up a court page and then a soldier fond of chivalric romances. In 1521 a French cannonball shattered his leg at the siege of Pamplona. He spent long months recovering, read the only two books in the castle, and emerged a different man. He went on to found the Society of Jesus with six companions in a chapel at Montmartre in Paris. Source: Autobiography of Ignatius.

joan-of-arc-domremy-the-voices-and-the-s.context_blurb: At about thirteen, a farmer's daughter in the village of Domremy on the French-Lorraine border began hearing voices in her father's garden. One voice named itself the Archangel Michael; the other two said they were early-Church women martyrs. At seventeen she convinced the local French captain Robert de Baudricourt to send her to the Dauphin's court at Chinon, and from there to the siege of Orleans. She rode in men's clothing and carried a white banner painted with 'Jhesus Maria.' Source: Trial transcripts; Chronicles of Jean Chartier.

joan-of-arc-the-trial-the-flames-and-hol.context_blurb: In May 1430 Joan of Arc rode out of the besieged town of Compiegne to attack an enemy camp. Her rearguard was cut off, the drawbridge closed too early behind her, and she was pulled from her horse into the hands of the Burgundian faction, who sold her to the English. She was tried for heresy by the French-collaborationist bishop Pierre Cauchon at Rouen through the winter and spring of 1431 and burned at the stake in the market-square there on 30 May. A sympathetic Dominican friar named Isambard de la Pierre held a cross for her as she died. Source: Trial transcripts; Rehabilitation trial.

john-hus-at-constance-in-a-hundred-years.context_blurb: Around 1400 a priest in Prague filled a chapel of about 3,000 townspeople week after week by preaching in the everyday Czech speech of the streets, when almost every other pulpit in Europe used Latin for sermons. Hus demanded reform of the Church and attacked the sale of indulgences. In 1414 he was summoned to the Council of Constance under an imperial safe-conduct, which was then torn up. He was condemned as a heretic and burned at the stake on 6 July 1415. His last recorded words contained a famous prediction. Source: Petr of Mladonovice, Account of the Trial of Jan Hus.

john-of-the-cross-the-dark-night-of-the-.context_blurb: In the Castilian town of Medina del Campo a small brilliant friar, barely five feet tall, is preparing in 1567 to leave the Carmelites for the stricter Carthusians when a determined fifty-two-year-old nun — Teresa of Avila — buttonholes him and talks him into launching her reform among the men instead. The two together began what became the Discalced Carmelites. The great mystical poetry he wrote in a nine-month imprisonment by the opposing Carmelite faction in Toledo — 'The Dark Night of the Soul,' 'The Spiritual Canticle' — made him one of the great Spanish poets. Source: John of the Cross, poetry and prose.

julian-of-norwich-all-shall-be-well.context_blurb: In May 1373, in an English city on the eastern coast, a woman about thirty and a half years old lay dying of a mysterious illness. A priest at her bedside held up a wooden cross so her fading eyes could rest on it — and instead of dying she began to see visions. She recovered, lived decades more as an anchoress walled into a small cell against a parish church, and wrote two versions of her Revelations of Divine Love — the earliest surviving book in English by a named woman author. T. S. Eliot would quote one of her lines in Four Quartets. Source: Revelations of Divine Love.

teresa-of-avila-the-transverberation-and.context_blurb: In 1515 a merchant family in the walled Castilian city of Avila welcomed a daughter, Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada. She would grow up to reform the Carmelite order, first as a member and then as foundress of its stricter Discalced branch, and to become the first woman named a Doctor of the Catholic Church. Her autobiography describes an experience she called her 'second conversion' and a famous vision of an angel plunging a flaming dart into her heart — the Transverberation Bernini later carved in marble. She also wrote the great mystical treatise The Interior Castle, structured around seven mansions. Source: Teresa, Vida and El Castillo Interior.

thomas-aquinas-the-ox-of-sicily-and-all-.context_blurb: Thomas Aquinas was born about 1225 to a noble family of southern Italy. When as a young man he insisted on joining the brand-new Dominican order, his family literally kidnapped him and held him in their castle for a year to change his mind. Freed at last, Thomas went north to study under the greatest teacher in Europe, Albertus Magnus. Because Thomas was huge, heavy, and almost silent in class, the other students mocked him with an animal nickname. He went on to write the gigantic Summa Theologiae and became the central theologian of the Catholic Church. Source: Vita Thomae; Gui, Vita.

thomas-becket-at-canterbury-four-knights.context_blurb: Thomas Becket and King Henry II of England were so close in the 1150s that they hunted, drank, and rode together like brothers, with Becket serving as the king's Chancellor. In 1162 the king rewarded his old companion with the Archbishopric of Canterbury, sure the old friend would keep the clergy in line. He was wrong. Six years of conflict ended on the evening of 29 December 1170 in Canterbury Cathedral, where a party of four knights rushed in. An eyewitness monk later wrote down everything he saw. Source: contemporary eyewitness accounts.

thomas-more-the-kings-good-servant-but-g.context_blurb: Thomas More, born in London in 1478, was a lawyer, a scholar, and a close friend of the Dutch humanist Erasmus. In 1516 he published a little Latin book describing an imaginary island of perfect politics, with a title he had just coined from Greek roots meaning 'no place.' He later served Henry VIII as Lord Chancellor. When Henry broke with Rome, More resigned, refused the king's new Oath of Supremacy, and was tried and beheaded in 1535. His last words on the scaffold have gone around the world. Source: William Roper, Life of Sir Thomas More.

wilfrid-and-the-synod-of-whitby-the-dati.context_blurb: In 664 CE, two very different Christianities were growing side by side in Anglo-Saxon England: a Celtic tradition descended from Iona, and a Roman tradition brought in from Rome by Augustine of Canterbury two generations before. They disagreed on how to calculate Easter and on how a monk should tonsure his hair. Northumbria's royal household itself was split — King Oswiu kept the Celtic date, his queen Eanfled kept the Roman — which produced an awkward annual Easter clash in the same palace. The Synod of Whitby settled it, under the pro-Roman abbot Wilfrid. Source: Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica 3.25.

bedivere-and-the-returning-of-excalibur.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the last battle of Arthur's reign is fought against his own son Mordred on a bare field where nearly every knight on both sides is killed. Arthur himself is mortally wounded there. He gives his most trusted surviving knight one last order: take Excalibur down to the water and throw it in. The famous ending of the Round Table, two attempts at obedience, and the arm clothed in white samite that rises from the lake all follow. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 21.

camelot-and-the-round-table.context_blurb: In the old British legends of King Arthur, the young king who pulled the sword from the stone has one favorite city. His court sits there, and his Knights of the Round Table feast in its great hall. In 1155 the Norman poet Wace, writing an Arthurian history in French verse, gave the plainest practical reason for the Table's circular shape — Arthur's father Uther Pendragon had suffered one ugly problem at every feast in his court, and the young Arthur meant to end it. The Round Table's story runs through Chretien de Troyes, through the holy quest for the Siege Perilous, and finally through the quarrel in Malory that brings the fellowship down. Sources: Wace, Roman de Brut; Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

excalibur-and-the-lady-of-the-lake.context_blurb: Early in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the young Arthur rides out with Merlin and meets a very tall, very proud king on the road who challenges him to single combat. The two fight until Arthur's first sword — the one he drew from the stone — shatters in his hand. Merlin leads the dazed king to a lake where an arm clothed in white samite rises from the water holding a second, more famous sword out above the surface. The sword's scabbard will matter as much as the blade itself. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 1.

galahad-the-perfect-knight-and-the-siege.context_blurb: In the last books of Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, one young knight rides into Camelot on the feast of Pentecost in red armour, led by an old hermit, and takes an empty seat at the Round Table that had killed every other man who ever sat in it. In the story he is the pure knight who alone achieves the Holy Grail, together with Percival and Bors. His father is Lancelot and his mother is Elaine of Corbenic. He is the only knight to see the Grail in full. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books 13–17.

gareth-beaumains-the-kitchen-boy-who-was.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, a tall handsome young man arrives at Camelot at Pentecost and refuses to give his name. Sir Kay the seneschal, scorning him, gives him a mocking French nickname meaning 'Fair-Hands' and puts him to work scrubbing pots. A year later he rides out as a knight on a mission to rescue a lady named Lyonesse from a tyrant called the Red Knight of the Red Lands. His real identity is far higher than the kitchen boy anyone had assumed. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 7.

gawain-and-the-green-knight-the-beheadin.context_blurb: On New Year's Day at Camelot, King Arthur's court is at feast in the great hall when a huge stranger rides in on horseback. Everything about the man and the horse is one single startling colour — his skin, his beard, his armour, and the horse under him are all the same shade. He proposes a Christmas game to the knights of the Round Table. The young nephew of the king takes him up on it, and the whole fourteenth-century alliterative poem that follows is a test of chivalry. Source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (anonymous, c. 1375).

guinevere-the-queen-at-the-stake.context_blurb: The queen of Arthur's Camelot, whose long secret love-affair with one of Arthur's greatest knights finally shatters the fellowship she had been given as a wedding-gift from her father, has a name that has passed into English from a Welsh original meaning roughly 'white phantom.' Mordred and Agravain trap her with her lover in her chamber one night, and the escape costs many knights' lives. Arthur must sentence her to burn, her lover rescues her at the last moment, and the kingdom falls apart. She ends her life in a Wessex nunnery. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Books 20–21.

kay-the-seneschal-the-sharp-tongued-fost.context_blurb: In the Arthurian legends, one knight is Arthur's foster-brother: they grew up together in the same household believing they were natural brothers, before the sword-in-the-stone revealed Arthur's true parentage. He is the son of Sir Ector, Arthur's foster-father, and he becomes Arthur's seneschal — the household officer in charge of the court. In Malory he is a sharp-tongued and often rude knight, but the Welsh tradition in Culhwch and Olwen makes him far grander, giving him magical powers and nine days without sleep. Source: Malory; Culhwch and Olwen.

lancelot-of-the-lake-the-greatest-knight.context_blurb: After his father King Ban of Benwick dies of his wounds fleeing a burning castle, an infant is stolen from his mother's arms by a fairy — the Lady of the Lake — who carries him down into her enchanted underwater realm and raises him there. He grows up to be the greatest knight of Arthur's Round Table and the queen's secret lover. His love-affair with Guinevere and his madness in the forest for two years after Elaine of Corbenic tricks him both figure in Malory, as does the final scene where angels lift him to heaven at his death. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

merlin-the-mage-the-wizard-who-arranges-.context_blurb: At the young Arthur's court an old white-bearded man in a long robe advises the king on every disaster before it comes, arranges Arthur's own conception at Tintagel, sets up the sword-in-the-stone test to prove him rightful king, and in Geoffrey of Monmouth tells how a tower would not stand because two dragons were fighting beneath it. In Malory's telling he is sometimes called 'a devil's son.' He has one great weakness that he foresees and cannot avoid. Source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae; Malory.

merlins-end-the-enchantress-in-the-rock.context_blurb: In his old age the great wizard of Arthur's court falls in love with a beautiful young damsel of the Lady of the Lake's kin and follows her wherever she goes like a lovesick fool. He cannot leave her side. He teaches her every magical secret he knows, and when she has learned enough she uses the last of those secrets against him. In Malory she is Nimue (also spelled Nimueh or Niviane). The place where she buries him alive is the Breton forest of Broceliande. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 4.

mordred-and-the-battle-of-camlann.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the young King Arthur one night sleeps with a queen who is a guest at his court, not knowing that she is his own half-sister. She conceives a son by him that night. Years later that son rides as a knight of the Round Table, foments the quarrel over Guinevere and Lancelot that shatters the fellowship, seizes the throne while Arthur is away in France, and finally faces him on the battlefield of Camlann. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 21; Annales Cambriae.

morgan-le-fay-the-half-sister-who-steals.context_blurb: Arthur has three older half-sisters, all daughters of his mother Igraine by her first husband Duke Gorlois of Cornwall, born before Igraine ever married Uther Pendragon. The most dangerous of the three is a sorceress — married to King Uriens of Gore, mother of Yvain, and bitter enemy of her brother Arthur. She steals Excalibur's scabbard, which protects its wearer from bleeding, and tries to kill Arthur and Guinevere by various enchantments. At the end she is one of the queens who carry Arthur away to Avalon. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

perceval-and-the-fisher-king-the-questio.context_blurb: A country boy is raised alone in the wilds of Wales by his widowed mother. She keeps him deliberately ignorant of what knights are and what knighthood means — because her husband and her elder sons were all killed as knights, and she cannot bear to lose him the same way. This boy will grow up to be one of the Round Table's great knights and the first to glimpse the Grail. In Chretien de Troyes's unfinished Perceval le Gaulois the Grail procession passes before him and he fails to ask the question that would have healed the Fisher King. Source: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval.

the-barge-to-avalon-the-once-and-future-.context_blurb: King Arthur is dying after his last battle against Mordred at Camlann. He gives his most trusted surviving knight one last order: take Excalibur down to the water and throw it in. After the sword is returned to the Lady of the Lake, a black barge glides to the shore carrying three queens in black. They lay the wounded king on it with his head in a queen's lap, and sail him away. Later tradition says the barge carried him to Avalon — the Isle of Apples — and that his grave is in Glastonbury. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 21.

the-grail-as-the-cup-of-the-last-supper-.context_blurb: In the earliest Grail stories the holy cup is simply a mysterious vessel seen in a procession, and no one explains what it is. In the early thirteenth century one French poet first identified it with the cup used at Jesus's final meal with his disciples, in which a wealthy follower afterwards caught drops of blood at the crucifixion. In that version the same follower then travels west with it to the British Isles. In the German retelling by Wolfram von Eschenbach the Grail is instead something else entirely. Sources: early French and German Grail poems.

the-grail-procession-bleeding-lance-swor.context_blurb: The first thing to enter the supper hall in Chretien de Troyes's Perceval procession is a young man carrying a weapon that looks like an ordinary spear except for one uncanny detail — a single drop keeps falling from its tip without stopping. A silver platter and a sword follow it, and last of all comes a radiant covered dish of gold. Perceval watches it pass by without asking a single question, which is the one thing he was supposed to do. Source: Chretien de Troyes, Perceval le Gaulois.

the-round-table-fellowship-knights-quest.context_blurb: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, King Arthur has a great round wooden table set up at Camelot where his chosen knights sit as equals, none at the head. Every year on the high feast of Pentecost they ride in to Camelot together to renew their vows of knighthood. Their code — the Pentecostal Oath — binds them to always help a lady in need, never to murder, and above all to give mercy to any who asks mercy. The fellowship rises to a hundred and fifty and finally fractures over the queen's affair with Lancelot. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur.

the-sword-in-the-stone-whoso-pulleth-out.context_blurb: Uther Pendragon, King of Britain, has died leaving no acknowledged heir, and the barons are ready to fight each other for the crown. In Malory Book I, Merlin tells the Archbishop of Canterbury to summon every lord in the land to London by Christmas so that God can show a sign. In a churchyard they find a huge stone with a sword driven into it and an inscription in gold around the hilt. Only one person in all Britain can pull the sword from the stone — and it turns out not to be anyone the barons expected. Source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur Book 1.

tristan-and-iseult-the-love-potion-and-t.context_blurb: In the old Cornish romance, a young knight of Lyonesse is sent by his uncle the King of Cornwall to sail to Ireland and bring back the Irish princess Iseult the Fair as a bride — not for himself, but for his uncle. On the voyage back he and the princess accidentally drink a love-potion her mother had prepared for the wedding night. The whole rest of their lives are shadowed by that drink. They are discovered, condemned, flee into a forest, and finally Tristan dies waiting for a sail of a particular colour. Sources: Beroul; Thomas of Britain; Gottfried von Strassburg.

uther-pendragon-and-igraine-conception-a.context_blurb: Long before Arthur is born, a king of Britain sits at a great banquet at his court and sees the beautiful wife of one of his own dukes. He falls violently in love with her on the spot. With Merlin's magic he enters her castle at Tintagel on the Cornish coast disguised as her husband and spends the night with her, while the real husband is killed on a raid elsewhere. The child conceived that night will become the greatest king in Britain's legendary history. Source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae; Malory.

wolframs-parzival-the-grail-as-a-stone-f.context_blurb: In the first quarter of the 1200s a Bavarian knight-poet sat down to retell, in Middle High German, an unfinished French Grail-poem by Chretien de Troyes. He turned it into an epic of about 25,000 rhymed lines that became the greatest German Arthurian romance. In his version the Holy Grail is not a cup at all; it is kept by a brotherhood of knights at the castle Munsalvaesche, and new names appear on it each year on a specific high feast of the Christian calendar. The hero's half-brother is black-and-white speckled. Source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival.

aengus-and-the-dream-the-swan-maiden-of-.context_blurb: The old Irish Aislinge Oenguso ('The Dream of Aengus') tells how the young love-god of the Tuatha De Danann falls asleep in his great mound Bru na Boinne on the Boyne and dreams every night of the most beautiful woman he has ever seen. He falls sick with longing. His whole family of the Tuatha De finally search Ireland for her, and the search ends on a lake in the west where a company of women is gathered, paired by chains of silver. A feast of Samhain, a transformation, and a famous Old Irish pun on 'a day and a night' bring the story to its end. Sources: Aislinge Oenguso; Dindsenchas.

balor-of-the-evil-eye-and-the-eyelid-fou.context_blurb: In Irish myth the sea-monster people who lived in Ireland before the Tuatha De Danann arrived — misshapen, often one-legged and one-eyed, and cruel — were the enemies of every wave of settlers. Their king at the Second Battle of Moytura is the most terrible figure in the whole tradition. He has a single giant eye on his forehead so poisonous that whatever it looked upon dropped dead; four men are needed just to lift his eyelid. His own daughter's son is prophesied to kill him. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

boann-and-the-river-boyne-the-well-of-se.context_blurb: The River Boyne in County Meath runs past the great neolithic burial mound of Newgrange and out to the Irish Sea. In Irish myth the river is the body of a Tuatha De Danann goddess who drowned at its source and became the water. The medieval Metrical Dindshenchas tells how she walked round a forbidden Well of Segais in the wrong direction and the water burst up and chased her all the way to the sea. Hazel trees of knowledge drop their nuts into the pool. Source: Metrical Dindsenchas.

bres-the-beautiful-the-half-fomorian-tyr.context_blurb: After the Tuatha De god-king Nuada lost his hand in battle and had to give up the throne (Irish law forbade a blemished king), the Tuatha De chose a new king known as the handsomest man of his generation. He was 'the Beautiful.' His blood was half Tuatha De and half Fomorian, chosen to keep the peace. His short reign ended in a famous insult over a meagre meal at court, which produced the first satire ever made in Ireland. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

brigid-of-the-tuatha-poetry-healing-smit.context_blurb: One of the greatest goddesses of the Tuatha De Danann is a daughter of the Dagda. She is the patron of three crafts at once — poetry, healing, and the making of weapons at the forge — so the Irish call her by three matching titles: 'of the Poets,' 'of the Healers,' 'of the Smiths.' Her feast is at the first of February, the old Irish beginning of spring. In Christian times she shares her name with Brigid of Kildare. Source: Cormac's Glossary; Cath Maige Tuired.

lugh-at-tara-the-doorkeepers-list-of-art.context_blurb: In Irish myth, a young warrior in a gold king's diadem came to the gates of Tara during King Nuada's feast, leading a company of warriors and asking to be let in. The doorkeeper refused him unless he had a skill the court did not already have. The young stranger named art after art — carpenter, smith, warrior, harper, poet, physician, cup-bearer — and for each the doorkeeper named a Tuatha De master of that skill. Then he asked whether the court had a single man who was all of these at once. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

manannan-mac-lir-the-wave-sweeper-enbarr.context_blurb: In Irish myth Manannan mac Lir is the god of the sea, ruler of the Isle of Apples (Emain Ablach, the Irish cousin of Avalon), and keeper of a cluster of magical treasures. His horse Enbarr of the Flowing Mane runs on sea and land alike; his cloak of invisibility hides him from sight; his sword Fragarach, the Answerer, could cut through any armor and compel a bound man to speak only truth. The Feast of Goibniu held in his undersea halls keeps the Tuatha De from aging. Sources: Cormac's Glossary; Immram Brain.

midir-and-etain-a-fly-a-hundred-years-a-.context_blurb: The Tochmarc Etaine, 'The Wooing of Etain,' is one of the most intricate stories in all Irish myth. A Tuatha De god of a sidhe mound at Bri Leith falls in love with the most beautiful mortal woman ever born in Ireland and marries her. His first jealous Tuatha De wife turns the bride into an insect and blows her out of the house with a storm, driving the whole long cycle of transformations and rebirths that follows. Centuries later a High King of Ireland wins the bride back a second time — and the god comes for her again at a Tara board-game. Source: Tochmarc Etaine.

newgrange-aengus-tricks-the-dagda-out-of.context_blurb: On a bend of a river in County Meath, Irish farmers five thousand years ago raised a great round mound of white quartz and dark stone, with a passage running deep inside it. In Irish myth this mound was the palace of the Dagda, chief of the Tuatha De Danann. His youngest son Aengus tricks him out of it with a famous Old Irish wordplay on 'a day and a night.' Two other huge mounds — Knowth and Dowth — stand nearby. Source: Tochmarc Etaine; archaeology of the Boyne Valley.

nuada-silver-hand-the-king-who-lost-a-th.context_blurb: In Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland from four northern cities, and the first king to lead them onto the island carried a burning blade called the Sword of Light — once drawn from its sheath, no enemy could escape it. He lost his right arm at the shoulder at the First Battle of Moytura, which under Irish law disqualified him from kingship. The healer Dian Cecht and the wright Creidhne made him a working silver hand so he could reclaim his throne. His own son Miach made him a better one, and paid the price. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

nuadas-death-at-moytura-and-lughs-kingsh.context_blurb: As the Tuatha De Danann prepared for their great war against the Fomorians, the true king Nuada Silverhand did an unusual thing: he stepped off his own throne and put a younger champion in his place for the run-up to the battle. The young champion was Lugh of the Long Arm — a master of every art. Thirteen days later at the Second Battle of Moytura, Lugh brought down Balor of the Evil Eye with a single slingshot. The Morrigan then chanted the Fomorians off the field. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-children-of-lir-nine-hundred-years-a.context_blurb: In Irish myth a Tuatha De figure named Lir lost his first wife and married her sister Aoife to be a mother to his four small children. The new stepmother grew jealous of how much Lir loved the children and, on the edge of a lake, turned all four of them into swans with a druid's rod. Her curse kept them in that shape for nine hundred years, flying through three hundred-year sentences on three different stretches of water. Their long story is one of the Three Sorrows of Storytelling. Source: Oidheadh Chlainne Lir.

the-dagda-his-club-his-harp-his-cauldron.context_blurb: In Irish myth a huge, red-bearded, big-bellied god in a hooded cloak is the chief of the Tuatha De Danann. His people call him 'good' — not because he is kindly, but because he is skilled at every craft: war, magic, poetry, husbandry, cooking. He owns the Lorg Mor — a great club that killed with one end and brought back to life with the other — a cauldron that fed any gathering until all were satisfied, and a magical harp named Daur Da Bla. He lives in Bru na Boinne on the Boyne. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-fir-bolg-the-bag-men-and-the-five-pr.context_blurb: The Lebor Gabala Erenn, the Irish Book of Invasions, lists six waves of settlers who came to Ireland one after another. Right before the Tuatha De Danann arrived, one older people held the whole island. According to the Book of Invasions they were descendants of the earlier Nemedians who had been driven out of Ireland by the Fomorians and spent generations as earth-slaves in Greece before coming home. They divided Ireland into its traditional five provinces and ruled under their king Eochaid mac Eirc. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-fomorians-sea-monster-people-one-leg.context_blurb: Before any of the six waves of settlers arrived in Ireland, a dark race already lived on the rocky islands and coasts and made war on every incoming people — the primordial enemies of Partholon, Nemed, and finally the Tuatha De Danann. They are often described as misshapen — one eye, one arm, one leg — and cruel. Their shape in Irish myth echoes the giants (the Jotnar) of Norse myth who ring the gods' world in the same way. The second great battle at Moytura ends their rule. Sources: Lebor Gabala Erenn; Cath Maige Tuired.

the-four-treasures-lia-fail-spear-of-lug.context_blurb: When the Tuatha De Danann arrived in Ireland, the tales say they brought a sacred set of magical objects with them — one from each of the four northern cities of learning where their druid-teachers had trained them. The treasures are the Stone of Destiny (the Lia Fail) from Falias, the invincible Spear of Lugh from Gorias, the Sword of Nuada from Findias, and the Cauldron of the Dagda from Murias. In every medieval Irish source they are counted exactly the same way. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-milesians-and-amergins-poem-i-am-a-w.context_blurb: In the medieval Book of Invasions, six waves of settlers reach Ireland in turn — Cessair, Partholon, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha De Danann, and one last people. This sixth and final wave sails in from Iberia and becomes the ancestors of the modern Irish Gaels. Their chief poet Amergin Gluingel ('White-Knee') speaks a famous nature-poem as he first sets his right foot on the Irish shore. The Milesians make a treaty with the defeated Tuatha De dividing Ireland between surface and underground. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-morrigan-at-the-ford-crow-prophecy-t.context_blurb: In old Irish myth a dark-winged bird was known to settle on shield-rims and spear-points as an army lined up for battle — and whichever side she chose was the side about to die. The Tuatha De Danann called this bird-shape one of their goddesses in the shape she liked best. She is a triple-goddess, sometimes paired with Macha and Badb, and she keeps a yearly tryst with the Dagda at the river Unius on the feast of Samhain. At the Second Battle of Moytura she chants the Fomorian king Indech off the field. Source: Cath Maige Tuired.

the-sidhe-mounds-and-the-aos-si-where-th.context_blurb: After the Tuatha De Danann went underground into the hollow hills, later Irish tradition stopped calling them 'the Tuatha De' at all — they became a new folk under a new name, the beings that English-speakers now call 'the fairies' or 'the Good Folk.' Their mounds are called the sidhe. On the feast of Samhain the veil between worlds thins and they walk among mortals; the hawthorn tree is held sacred to them, and the lone 'fairy thorn' in a field is left standing. Source: Irish folklore; Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-six-invasions-of-ireland-from-cessai.context_blurb: A medieval Irish book compiled in the eleventh century, the Lebor Gabala Erenn — 'the Book of the Taking of Ireland' — gives the island an origin story in successive waves of settlers, one after another, each taking the land from the last. The first wave was led by Cessair before the Flood; another survivor named Fintan mac Bochra lived through the Flood as a salmon and spans the whole book. The last wave is the Gaels. The book is a monk's attempt to fit Ireland's pre-Christian history into the frame of Genesis. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

the-tuatha-de-danann-the-god-people-of-d.context_blurb: Irish myth tells of a supernatural people who arrived in Ireland long before the modern Irish, and who are the closest thing Irish tradition has to a family of gods. Their name literally means 'the people of the goddess Danu' (or Ana). They land in a dark cloud on the mountains of Connacht and burn their own ships on the beach so that there is no going back. Among their chief figures are the Dagda, Lugh, the Morrigan, Nuada, and Manannan mac Lir. After the Milesians arrive they go underground into the hollow hills. Source: Lebor Gabala Erenn.

joseph-interprets-pharaohs-dreams-the-se.context_blurb: Years after being sold into slavery and later imprisoned in Egypt on a false charge, Joseph the son of Jacob is suddenly brought up out of the dungeon to stand before Pharaoh. Pharaoh has had two linked dreams no court magician can read — seven fat creatures come up out of the Nile and are swallowed up by seven lean ones. Joseph is to tell Pharaoh what the dreams mean and what to do about them. Source: Genesis 41 KJV.

dominic-and-the-black-and-white-habit.context_blurb: In the Castilian village of Caleruega around 1170, a noblewoman named Jane of Aza was pregnant with a son — the future Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican Order. Tradition says she dreamed one night that an animal ran out of her womb carrying a burning torch in its mouth and set the world on fire. Dominic later preached across southern France against the Cathar heretics, founded his order in a plain two-tone habit, and sent his first friars to the two great medieval universities. Three centuries later a young Michelangelo helped finish his tomb in Bologna. Source: Jordan of Saxony, Libellus de principiis OP.

bran-and-sceolang-fionns-hounds-who-were.context_blurb: In the Fenian tales of Ireland, Fionn mac Cumhaill leads the warrior-band called the Fianna and hunts across Ireland with a great pack of hounds. Two of his hounds are his favourites, named in every Fenian tale, and they can outrun any deer and understand what he says to them. The old stories insist they are not just clever dogs — Fionn's own aunt Uirne (also called Tuiren) had been turned into a hound by the people of the sidhe while she was carrying them, so the two pups were born under the enchantment with human kin among the Fianna. Source: Macgnimartha Finn; Fenian cycle.

cathbad-the-druid-and-the-prophecy-of-sh.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle the chief druid at the royal fort of Emain Macha runs a school for young pupils, teaching them to read what the days to come will bring. He is King Conchobar mac Nessa's adviser and, in one strand of the tradition, Conchobar's own father by the warrior-woman Nessa. His great prophecy over a young girl named Deirdre and his advice to the boy Setanta are both scenes that drive the whole cycle. Source: Longes mac nUislenn; Macgnimartha Con Culainn.

cu-chulainn-kills-his-own-son-connla-at-.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle, the greatest Irish warrior sails away as a young man to train in arms with a fearsome war-woman named Scathach on an island called the Isle of Shadow. While there, Scathach is at war with a rival warrior-queen named Aife. Cu Chulainn meets Aife in single combat and spares her life; she bears him a son and sends the boy back to Ireland years later with a gold thumb-ring and a geis never to give his name. The father meets the son in combat not knowing who he is. Scholars note parallel Indo-European tales of Rustam and Sohrab. Source: Aided Oenfhir Aife.

diarmuid-and-grainne-the-elopement-and-t.context_blurb: In the Fenian Cycle, the aging warrior-leader Fionn mac Cumhaill — now older than the High King himself — is promised in marriage to the young and beautiful daughter of Cormac mac Airt, the High King at Tara. One of Fionn's own finest young warriors wears a magical love-spot on his forehead that any mortal woman who glimpses it falls hopelessly in love with. At the betrothal feast the princess drugs the cups and makes him flee with her. The pursuit runs sixteen years across Ireland. Source: Toruigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne.

emer-and-the-wooing-cu-chulainns-wife-wh.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, one of the great foretales of the Tain is a courtship-story rather than a battle-tale: the greatest warrior of Ulster goes out and chooses the one young woman he will marry above every daughter of Ireland. He asks her riddles; she out-wits him with riddles of her own. Her father Forgall Manach then tries to kill him by sending him on the perilous training-journey to Scathach's island. Years later, Cu Chulainn's one great fairy-affair with the goddess Fand ends when his wife Emer chooses to give him up to her. Source: Tochmarc Emire.

ferdiad-at-the-ford-four-days-killing-a-.context_blurb: The Tain Bo Cuailnge tells of a young Ulster champion who holds off Queen Medb's whole invading army by killing her champions one after another at river fords. The darkest of these duels is a four-day combat against his own foster-brother Ferdiad, whom they had trained with Scathach as fellow pupils and who shares his horn-skin that no ordinary weapon can pierce. The fight is finally decided by the belly-spear cast with the foot — the Gae Bolg — in the river at Ardee in County Louth. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

fionn-mac-cumhaill-and-the-salmon-of-wis.context_blurb: The Fenian Cycle of Irish myth tells of a great hero who becomes chief of the Fianna, the roving warrior-band that guards the High King. As a boy named Deimne, he spent seven years as apprentice to an old poet named Finnegas, who had been fishing a certain pool on the Boyne for twenty years waiting to catch one specific salmon — the Salmon of Wisdom, which had grown wise by eating nine hazelnuts that fell into the Well of Segais. The way the boy ended up with the fish's gift — through a burnt thumb and a quick instinctive gesture — gave him his new name. Source: Macgnimartha Finn.

fionn-sleeping-in-the-cave-the-once-and-.context_blurb: In one popular Irish folk-tradition, a great Irish warrior-chief does not have a death-tale at all. He is said to be lying inside a cave beneath an Irish hill, surrounded by all his sleeping warriors in full armour, waiting for the day Ireland needs him most. Beside him lies a horn of the Fianna that must be sounded a particular number of times to wake him. The parallel to King Arthur sleeping at Avalon is obvious. An 18th-century Scottish poet and a 19th-century German composer each drew on similar material for famous Romantic works. Source: Irish folklore.

loeg-mac-riangabra-and-the-grey-of-macha.context_blurb: On the morning of the fatal battle in the Aided Con Culainn, the hero's charioteer goes out as usual to yoke the chariot. But Cu Chulainn's famous horse the Grey of Macha will not let him. The horse turns his left side three times against the charioteer and refuses the harness; only when Cu Chulainn himself comes out does the horse consent — and even then weeps tears of blood onto his master's feet. The charioteer Loeg mac Riangabra, called the 'king of chariot-drivers,' is one of the most beloved of Cu Chulainn's companions and dies beside him at the end. Source: Aided Con Culainn.

oisin-in-tir-na-nog-niamh-of-the-golden-.context_blurb: In the Fenian tale, Fionn's poet-son is carried away over the sea by a woman of the Sidhe named Niamh of the Golden Hair to live on a distant island paradise where he will never grow old. He stays for what feels like three years. When he asks to go home to Ireland, Niamh lets him ride her horse Embarr of the Flowing Mane, warning that his feet must never touch Irish soil. Back in Ireland he finds three hundred years have passed; everyone he loved is dead. Then a strap breaks. The man who finds him is Saint Patrick. Source: Agallamh na Seanorach.

scathach-and-the-isle-of-shadow-cu-chula.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the greatest teacher of arms in the world is not a druid or a king but a warrior-woman who runs a martial school on a stormy island off the coast of Alba. She takes the boy-hero Cu Chulainn as her pupil. On her island — identified in later tradition with the Isle of Skye — he learns the salmon-leap and twenty-six other feats of arms, meets his future wife Emer's challenger Ferdiad as a fellow pupil, and is given the Gae Bolg. Source: Tochmarc Emire.

setanta-and-the-hound-of-culann-the-boy-.context_blurb: The greatest hero of the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth is not born under the name he dies under. As a boy at Dun Dealgan (modern Dundalk) he is called Setanta — a nephew of King Conchobar mac Nessa, born to Conchobar's sister Deichtine. His father in the divine order is the god Lugh Lamhfhada. The way he gets his adult name is a famous scene: as a boy on his way to a feast at the smith Culann's house, with only a hurling-stick and ball in his hand, he meets the smith's great war-hound head-on. The boy's reward is the smith's new name. Source: Macgnimartha Con Culainn; Tain Bo Cuailnge.

the-cattle-raid-of-cooley-medb-ailill-an.context_blurb: The whole plot of the Irish epic the Tain Bo Cuailnge is set in motion by an argument in their royal bed at Cruachan — Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband King Ailill count up their possessions one evening and discover that Ailill owns a magnificent white-horned bull she has no equal for in her own herd. She determines to steal a rival bull from Ulster to match it. Medb sends ambassadors; her messengers, drunk, boast that they would take the bull by force if refused; the owner refuses; and the great Cattle Raid is on. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.

the-champions-portion-at-bricrius-feast-.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle a sharp-tongued poet is so hated for his mischief that when he throws a great feast the warriors will only agree to come if he sits apart in a separate raised gallery, so his poison-verses cannot reach them across the hall. At that feast he stirs up a quarrel between three Ulster champions over who deserves the Champion's Portion of the roast — including a beheading-game with a huge rough herdsman carrying an axe that is the clearest ancestor of the Sir Gawain and the Green Knight story. Source: Fled Bricrenn.

the-curse-of-macha-why-the-ulstermen-lay.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle a supernatural woman comes to live secretly with a widowed farmer named Crunniuc. She blesses his household with prosperity and asks only that he never boast about her to strangers. At King Conchobar's assembly Crunniuc gets drunk and boasts anyway. The king, insulted, forces the woman — nine months pregnant — to race the king's chariot-horses. She wins the race and gives birth on the finish-line. Her dying curse lays the warriors of Ulster, from the ninth generation on, under the pangs of a woman in labour every time an enemy army comes near. That is why Cu Chulainn stands alone. Source: Noinden Ulad.

the-death-of-cu-chulainn-tied-standing-t.context_blurb: The Ulster Cycle names one hero above all — a young warrior of twenty-seven trained on the Isle of Shadow, master of the belly-spear, and the only Ulsterman who fights on when the rest of the province lies helpless under the Curse of Macha. He dies at the end of the cycle's death-tale, the Aided Con Culainn. In that last scene he lashes himself upright to a standing-stone at Clochafarmore in County Louth so that he will die on his feet, and a raven lands on his shoulder only when the hero-light has gone out of him. In 1911 the Oliver Sheppard statue of this death would stand in Dublin's General Post Office for the 1916 Easter Rising. Source: Aided Con Culainn.

the-fianna-entry-tests-and-the-outsize-w.context_blurb: In the Fenian Cycle of Irish myth a roving warrior-band lives in the wild forests of Ireland by season, sworn to defend the High King against foreign invaders in war and to hunt and feast in peace. Their leader is Fionn mac Cumhaill. The entry-tests to join the Fianna were legendary — a candidate had to defend himself with only a shield and a hazel stick against nine warriors throwing spears at him from a distance of nine furrows, to run through a forest without disturbing a plait of his hair, and to leap and stoop under branches at full speed. The poet Caoilte mac Ronain survives to the time of Saint Patrick. Source: Agallamh na Seanorach.

the-gae-bolg-the-belly-spear-cast-with-t.context_blurb: In the Ulster Cycle of Irish myth, the hero Cu Chulainn carries one signature weapon that Queen Medb's warriors dread above every sword he owns — a spear given to him by his teacher on the Isle of Shadow, and the weapon he saves for the fights he is losing. It is cast from between the toes of the foot in the water and, once inside a body, opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb. The flesh has to be cut open around it to remove it. Its first mortal victim is his foster-brother Ferdiad; its last is Cu Chulainn himself, run through by his own weapon in the hands of the sons of Cailitin. Source: Tain Bo Cuailnge.
